questions.stem: A counter reads 92 counts/min with a source and 12 counts/min with the source removed. After 18 h the total reading is 22 counts/min. Find the half-life.
questions.explanation: The source alone drops from 80 to 10 counts/min, a factor of 8 or three halvings. Do not apply the halving rule to the background.

questions.stem: A fixed mass of gas at constant temperature has pressure 90 kPa and volume 24 cm³. It expands to 36 cm³ and then contracts to 18 cm³. Which row gives the pressures after expansion; after contraction (kPa)?
questions.explanation: The product pV stays 90 × 24 at both stages. Use the respective volumes as divisors, rather than assuming pressure is proportional to volume.

questions.stem: A pulse reflects from a wall. A microphone beside the sender picks up the echo 0.12 s after emission. Sound travels at 330 m/s. The wall moves 3.3 m farther away before a second pulse is emitted. What is the second echo delay?
questions.explanation: The extra path is 6.6 m because the pulse travels out and back. This takes 0.02 s, so add that to the first delay.

questions.stem: A trolley’s position is recorded as 1 m at 0 s, 5 m at 2 s, 5 m at 4 s and 1 m at 6 s. Between readings its position–time graph is straight. At which pair of times does it have the same speed but opposite velocities?
questions.explanation: The first segment has gradient +2 m/s, the middle is horizontal and the final segment has gradient −2 m/s. Only 1 s and 5 s lie on opposite sloping segments.

questions.stem: A lift is moving at constant speed upward. Which is greater: a rider’s weight or the upward force of the floor on the rider?
questions.explanation: Constant velocity means zero resultant force, even when the rider is moving. The opposing forces balance.

questions.stem: A 0.4 kg cart speeds up from 3 m/s to 8 m/s in the same direction. Find the magnitude of the impulse.
questions.explanation: Impulse is the change in momentum, 0.4(8 − 3), not the final momentum.

questions.stem: A walker moving at 2 m/s speeds up uniformly to 6 m/s in 5 s. Which row gives acceleration (m/s²); distance covered (m)?
questions.explanation: The speed change is 4 m/s over 5 s. Mean speed during uniform acceleration is (2 + 6)/2, giving 20 m.

questions.stem: A 6 kg crate is pulled horizontally with 32 N and accelerates at 3 m/s². The same resistance later acts when the pull falls to 8 N. Which row gives resistance (N); new acceleration in the pull direction (m/s²)?
questions.explanation: The first resultant is 18 N, so resistance is 14 N. With the weaker pull the resultant is −6 N and acceleration is −1 m/s².

questions.stem: A cart of mass 3 kg approaches a 1 kg cart at rest at 4 m/s. They stick. Find their common speed and state where the momentum went.

options.label: A
options.text: 4 m/s; it stayed in the system

options.label: F
options.text: 3 m/s; it stayed in the two-cart system

questions.explanation: Initial momentum 12 kg m/s is conserved for the pair, so divide it by the combined mass 4 kg. Kinetic energy need not be conserved.

questions.stem: A train initially at rest accelerates uniformly at 2 m/s² for 6 s. What is its displacement during those 6 s?
questions.explanation: Use s = ½at² from rest. Multiplying final speed by time would treat the train as moving that fast throughout.

questions.stem: Two crates, 2 kg and 3 kg, are joined by a light taut cord on a level floor. A 25 N pull on the 3 kg crate moves both. Each crate experiences a 5 N opposing force. Find the tension.
questions.explanation: Net force on both is 15 N and acceleration is 3 m/s². The 2 kg crate needs a net 6 N, so the tension must also overcome its 5 N resistance.

questions.stem: A velocity starts at +6 m/s and changes uniformly to −2 m/s over 8 s. Which row gives distance travelled (m); displacement (m)?
questions.explanation: Velocity crosses zero after 6 s. The areas have magnitudes 18 and 2; add for distance, subtract for displacement.

questions.stem: A 1 kg trolley moving east at 9 m/s collides with a 2 kg trolley moving west at 3 m/s. Afterward the first trolley moves west at 1 m/s. Which row gives the second trolley’s velocity (east positive, m/s); change in total kinetic energy (J)?
questions.explanation: Initial momentum is +3, so the second trolley has +4 kg m/s after the first takes −1. The initial kinetic energy is 49.5 J and final energy is 4.5 J.

questions.stem: A stage lift raises a prop at a steady speed and then lowers it at the same speed through the same distance. The platform pushes upward on the prop throughout. Compare the work done by this upward force on the prop in the two journeys.

options.label: A
options.text: The work is positive in both journeys.

options.label: B
options.text: The work is negative in both journeys.

options.label: C
options.text: The work is zero in both journeys.

options.label: D
options.text: Only the upward journey involves nonzero work by this force.

options.label: E
options.text: The work has equal magnitude and opposite sign.

options.label: F
options.text: Only the downward journey involves nonzero work by this force.

questions.explanation: At constant speed the upward force equals the prop’s weight on each journey. It acts with the displacement when rising and against it when descending, so the work changes sign but not magnitude.

questions.stem: Two objects have the same kinetic energy. Object B has four times the mass of A. How does B’s speed compare to A’s?
questions.explanation: For fixed kinetic energy, four times the mass requires one quarter of the squared speed. Take the square root.

questions.stem: A 100 N/m spring is extended by 8 cm within its elastic range. Find its stored energy.
questions.explanation: Convert 8 cm to 0.08 m and use ½kx². Without the half you would use the final force for the entire extension.

questions.stem: A rider and cycle of total mass 80 kg lose 9 m of height while speed rises from 4 to 10 m/s. Use g = 10 m/s². Which row gives loss of gravitational energy; gain in kinetic energy (J)?
questions.explanation: The gravitational loss is mgh. The kinetic gain is half the mass times the difference of squared speeds, not the square of their difference.

questions.stem: A 75%-efficient machine gives 240 J of useful work. Find the input energy and wasted energy in that order.
questions.explanation: Input is 240/0.75 = 320 J. The wasted amount is input minus useful output.

questions.stem: A 50 kg person climbs 6 m vertically in 12 s, starting and finishing at rest. Use g = 10 m/s². Find the average rate of gain of gravitational potential energy.
questions.explanation: The energy gain is 50 × 10 × 6 = 3000 J. Rate is energy divided by the 12 s elapsed.

questions.stem: The load on a spring rises from 4 N to 12 N within the Hooke’s-law range. Extension rises from 2 cm to 6 cm. Find the spring constant.
questions.explanation: Stiffness is the 8 N load change divided by 0.04 m, not by 4 cm with unchanged units.

questions.stem: A 2 kg sled reaches 6 m/s from rest while descending 3 m. The constant opposing force is 4 N. Use g = 10 m/s². Find the distance travelled down the slope.
questions.explanation: Gravitational energy lost is 60 J, while only 36 J appears as kinetic energy. The 24 J difference is the work against the 4 N force.

questions.stem: A conveyor moves a package 12 m at constant speed in 8 s. It supplies 54 W to overcome friction. Which row gives friction (N); work against it (J)?
questions.explanation: Work is 54 × 8 = 432 J. Dividing work by 12 m gives force, or equivalently power divided by speed.

questions.stem: Two Hooke’s-law springs store the same energy. Spring B stretches twice as far as spring A. Which row gives B’s stiffness; B’s stretching force as fractions of A’s?
questions.explanation: For equal ½kx², twice the extension requires one quarter the stiffness. The force kx is then half as large.

questions.stem: An ammeter on a charging circuit reads 0.30 A for the first 10 s and 0.10 A for the next 30 s. Current flows in the same direction throughout. How much charge passes in total?
questions.explanation: The charge is the area under the current–time graph: (0.30 × 10) + (0.10 × 30) = 6 C.

questions.stem: A 9 V cell supplies 3 C through a device. How much energy is transferred to the device?
questions.explanation: Voltage is energy per unit charge, so energy is 9 × 3 J.

questions.stem: In bright light the resistance of an LDR is smaller than in dim light. When connected directly to a fixed-voltage supply, what happens to the current as light increases?
questions.explanation: Current is V/R, so the lower resistance takes more current at fixed voltage. The polarity does not change.

questions.stem: Resistors of 3 Ω and 5 Ω share a 16 V supply in series. Which row gives the 5 Ω resistor’s voltage (V); share of the total electrical power?
questions.explanation: In series the same current flows through both. The 5 Ω resistor takes five eighths of the voltage and, because P = IV, five eighths of the power.

questions.stem: A resistor dissipates 36 W at 12 V. If its resistance is unchanged, what power does it dissipate at 8 V?
questions.explanation: Power scales as voltage squared for fixed resistance. Multiply 36 by (8/12)² rather than by 8/12.

questions.stem: Two resistors in parallel draw 8 A in total from 12 V. One branch has a resistance of 2 Ω. Which row gives the other branch current (A); its resistance (Ω)?
questions.explanation: The known branch takes 6 A. The other takes 2 A at the full 12 V, so it has resistance 6 Ω.

questions.stem: A resistor carries 0.6 A with 3 V across it, and 1.0 A with 5 V across it. What do these two readings support?

options.label: C
options.text: Power is the same at the two points.

options.label: D
options.text: Resistance is the same at the two points.

questions.explanation: Each voltage divided by its own current is 5 Ω. This comparison does not establish constant resistance outside the measured range.

questions.stem: A 15 V supply feeds a 4 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 6 Ω and 3 Ω. Find the power in the 6 Ω branch.
questions.explanation: The pair is equivalent to 2 Ω, so it receives one third of 15 V. The 6 Ω branch has all 5 V across it, giving V²/R.

questions.stem: A 240 W appliance runs for 20 minutes and a 90 W lamp runs for 40 minutes. Which row gives their energy use separately, in kWh?
questions.explanation: Convert power to kW and times to hours. The two products are 0.24/3 and 0.09 × 2/3.

questions.stem: A 10 Ω heater carries current I for 60 s. The current is doubled for the next 30 s. What fraction of total energy is transferred in the second interval?
questions.explanation: The second interval has four times the power for half the time. Its energy is twice that of the first interval, which gives two thirds of the total.

questions.stem: An ideal transformer has 250 primary turns and 500 secondary turns. Find secondary voltage for an input of 8 V.
questions.explanation: The secondary has twice the turns, so its voltage doubles. The inverse ratio applies to the current, not the voltage.

questions.stem: A sound source vibrates faster without changing its amplitude. Which quality increases for a stationary listener?

options.label: D
options.text: Sound speed in the same medium

questions.explanation: Greater frequency raises pitch. With the same wave speed it reduces wavelength, and loudness is associated with amplitude.

questions.stem: Find the gauge pressure 3 m under water of density 1000 kg/m³. Use g = 10 m/s².
questions.explanation: Use the pressure contribution ρgh. Gauge pressure here excludes atmospheric pressure.

questions.stem: A nucleus has mass number 234 and atomic number 90. It emits one alpha and then one beta-minus particle. Which row gives final mass; atomic number?
questions.explanation: Alpha emission subtracts 4 from mass number and 2 from atomic number. Beta-minus adds one to atomic number with no mass-number change.

questions.stem: A sealed gas of fixed mass at constant temperature occupies 30 cm³ at 80 kPa. Which row gives pressure at 20 cm³; volume at 200 kPa?
questions.explanation: The pressure–volume product is 2400 kPa cm³. Divide it by the specified volume or pressure to find the matching quantity.

questions.stem: A heater delivers 12 kJ to a 0.50 kg block and its surroundings. Three quarters goes to the block and raises its temperature by 20 °C. Find the block’s specific heat capacity.
questions.explanation: The block receives 9000 J. Divide by its mass times its temperature rise, using only the energy it absorbs.

questions.stem: A magnet moves towards a coil and then back along the same path. Which observation should change when the magnet reverses direction?

options.label: C
options.text: The sign of the magnet’s pole

options.label: D
options.text: The need for a conducting coil

questions.explanation: Reversing the motion reverses the change in flux and the induced voltage. The magnet’s pole need not change.

questions.stem: A sample plus background gives 95 counts/min. Its half-life is 4 hours; after 8 hours the detector reads 35 counts/min. What is the background count rate?
questions.explanation: Two half-lives leave one quarter of the initial source rate. With background b, 35 = b + (95 − b)/4, giving b = 15.

questions.stem: A water wave crosses obliquely into a region where its speed becomes three quarters of its initial value. Which row gives new frequency; new wavelength as fractions of their original values?
questions.explanation: The boundary does not change the source frequency. Wavelength therefore changes in the same ratio as speed.

questions.stem: A 160 W heater melts 0.12 kg of solid already at its melting point in 5 minutes. Only 75% of input reaches the solid. Find its specific latent heat of fusion.
questions.explanation: Absorbed energy is 0.75 × 160 × 300 = 36000 J. Divide by 0.12 kg; the temperature stays constant during melting.

questions.stem: At 6 V a cabinet light transfers 24 J in 4 s. A student doubles the time the light is on without changing its potential difference or current. What happens to its mean power?
questions.explanation: The original power is 24 ÷ 4 = 6 W. At unchanged current and voltage, twice as much energy transfers over twice the time, so the power is still 6 W.

questions.stem: A current of 0.25 A passes through a 4 Ω resistor for 40 s. How much energy is transferred?
questions.explanation: Use I²R to get 0.25 W and multiply by time. Using IR instead gives voltage, not power.

questions.stem: An ideal cell supplies two identical lamps in series. The lamps are moved into parallel across the same cell. Each lamp is modelled as a fixed resistor. By what factor does total current rise?
questions.explanation: The equivalent resistance changes from 2R to R/2, a factor of four. The current changes by the inverse factor.

questions.stem: A 2 Ω resistor is replaced by a 5 Ω resistor in series with an unchanged 3 Ω resistor and a 40 V supply. Which row gives the old current; new voltage across the 3 Ω resistor?
questions.explanation: The old total resistance is 5 Ω, so current is 8 A. The new current is 5 A, so the unchanged resistor gets 15 V.

questions.stem: A 3 kW water heater runs for 12 minutes and a 0.6 kW heater runs for 50 minutes. Electricity costs 30 p per kWh. What is their combined cost?
questions.explanation: The heaters use 0.6 and 0.5 kWh. Add these before multiplying by the charge per kWh.

questions.stem: A fixed resistor and an NTC thermistor are in series on a fixed supply. The thermistor is heated. What happens to the voltage across the fixed resistor?
questions.explanation: The heated thermistor takes less series resistance, so current rises and the voltage across the fixed resistor increases.

questions.stem: A 6 Ω resistor is in parallel with a 12 Ω resistor. The pair is then placed in series with 2 Ω. Which row gives the resistance of the pair; of the whole network?
questions.explanation: In parallel add reciprocal resistances and invert. Then add the series resistance normally.

questions.stem: A 10 Ω resistor has 2 V across it initially. The voltage is tripled without changing the resistance. By what factor does power increase?
questions.explanation: Since P = V²/R, multiplying V by three multiplies P by nine.

questions.stem: A fuse is fitted to protect a mains cable from excessive current. Why is the fuse placed in the live wire rather than the neutral wire?

options.label: A
options.text: The fuse lowers the normal mains voltage.

options.label: B
options.text: Only the live wire normally carries current.

options.label: C
options.text: The neutral wire carries only DC.

options.label: D
options.text: It prevents any current from entering the earth wire.

options.label: E
options.text: When it blows, it disconnects the appliance from the live supply.

questions.explanation: Opening the live connection removes the high-potential supply from the appliance. An open neutral alone would leave it connected to live.

questions.stem: An 18 V ideal supply feeds a 3 Ω series resistor and a parallel pair. The supply current is 3 A. One parallel branch is 4 Ω. Find the other branch resistance.
questions.explanation: The total resistance is 6 Ω, so the pair is 3 Ω. Subtract the known branch conductance 1/4 from the pair’s 1/3 to obtain 1/12.

questions.stem: A sealed package weighs less on a planet where gravitational field strength is weaker. The same balance compares the package with standard masses by checking which side needs more mass to balance. What happens to the package’s measured mass and its weight?

options.label: C
options.text: Mass stays the same; weight decreases.

options.label: D
options.text: Mass decreases; weight stays the same.

options.label: E
options.text: Mass stays the same; weight increases.

questions.explanation: A weaker field reduces the weights of both the package and the comparison masses by the same factor, so the same masses balance. The weight itself, mg, decreases.

questions.stem: A parachutist descends at the new terminal speed after opening a parachute. Which statement about the forces is true?
questions.explanation: The new terminal speed is constant, so the upward drag balances downward weight.

questions.stem: A trolley covers 12 m in the first 3 s and 24 m in the next 4 s. What is its mean speed over both intervals?
questions.explanation: Use total distance divided by total time. An unweighted average of the interval speeds would ignore their different durations.

questions.stem: A 4 kg crate slides right. A 20 N force pulls right, a 6 N force pulls left, and friction has magnitude 2 N. Which row gives the resultant force (right positive, N); acceleration (m/s²)?
questions.explanation: Both the leftward pull and friction oppose the rightward motion. Subtract them before dividing by mass.

questions.stem: A car passes a marker at 18 m/s and decelerates uniformly at 3 m/s². At what distance beyond the marker does it first reach 6 m/s?
questions.explanation: Slowing by 12 m/s at 3 m/s² takes 4 s. Mean speed is 12 m/s, giving 48 m.

questions.stem: A ball moving left has a momentum magnitude of 5 kg m/s. Its direction reverses and the magnitude becomes 3 kg m/s. Find the magnitude of the impulse.
questions.explanation: With right positive the change is +3 − (−5). Subtracting magnitudes would miss the reversal.

questions.stem: A 40 kg cyclist and 10 kg cycle accelerate at 2 m/s². Their forward driving force is 140 N. Which row gives the opposing force; the driving force needed to maintain speed if that opposition stays constant?
questions.explanation: The accelerating resultant is 100 N, leaving 40 N opposition. At constant speed the driving force must equal that opposition.

questions.stem: A winch lowers a 30 kg load by 4 m at constant speed. Use g = 10 m/s². How much gravitational potential energy does the load lose?
questions.explanation: Its height falls by 4 m, so it loses mgh. Constant speed fixes kinetic energy, not gravitational energy.

questions.stem: The force–extension graph of a spring is a straight line through the origin. If its extension is tripled, how does the area under the graph up to that extension change?
questions.explanation: Both the base and the height of the triangular area triple. The area, equal to elastic energy, becomes nine times as large.

questions.stem: A vehicle accelerates from rest to speed v for 4 s, keeps v for 3 s, then brakes uniformly to rest for 6 s. The total distance is 96 m. What is its speed during the middle interval?
questions.explanation: The graph area is v times half of each sloped interval plus the full middle interval, or 8v. Set this to 96.

questions.stem: A uniform material is supplied as solid sheets of thickness 0.2 cm. A piece with area 30 cm² has mass 18 g. What mass would a solid piece with area 50 cm² and thickness 0.3 cm have?
questions.explanation: The first piece occupies 6 cm³ and so the density is 3 g/cm³. The second occupies 15 cm³, giving 45 g.

questions.stem: Two insulated containers hold the same mass of different liquids. Identical heaters deliver equal power. Liquid X warms by 12 °C in 4 minutes and liquid Y warms by 8 °C in 2 minutes. What is the ratio of the specific heat capacity of X to that of Y?
questions.explanation: With equal masses and powers, specific heat capacity is proportional to heating time divided by temperature change. The ratio is (4/12) : (2/8) = 4 : 3.

questions.stem: A gap between two surfaces is evacuated. Which mechanism can still transfer thermal energy directly across the gap?

options.label: D
options.text: Only the movement of hot gas particles

questions.explanation: Electromagnetic radiation needs no material medium. Gas conduction and convection cannot occur in the evacuated gap.

questions.stem: A stone of mass 450 g is submerged in a measuring cylinder. The water reading rises from 120 to 270 cm³. Which row gives stone volume; stone density?
questions.explanation: Its volume is the increase in reading, not the final reading. Divide 450 g by 150 cm³.

questions.stem: A gas at fixed temperature occupies 200 cm³ at 90 kPa. Its pressure is first doubled, then decreased by 30 kPa. What final volume does it occupy?
questions.explanation: The final pressure is 150 kPa, not 60 kPa. Divide the original pressure–volume product by 150.

questions.stem: Two equal masses A and B receive the same energy, with no losses. A warms by 12 °C and B by 4 °C. How does B’s specific heat capacity compare with A’s?
questions.explanation: At fixed mass and energy input, specific heat capacity is inversely proportional to temperature rise.

questions.stem: A heated sample takes in 900 J while remaining at its melting point. Its specific latent heat of fusion is 18000 J/kg. Which row gives the mass melted in kg; the energy needed to melt double that mass?
questions.explanation: Use m = E/L to get 0.05 kg. Latent heat scales linearly with mass, so double the energy as well.

questions.stem: An ultrasound pulse returns to a probe 0.004 s after transmission. The speed is 1500 m/s. How far is the reflecting surface from the probe?
questions.explanation: The travel time includes the outward and return journeys. Halve the distance found from speed times time.

questions.stem: Liquid X has twice the density of Y. At equal gauge pressure, how does the depth in X compare to that in Y?
questions.explanation: Pressure is proportional to density times depth at fixed g, so twice the density needs half the depth.

questions.stem: A heater takes 90 s to warm a block by 12 °C. It delivers 80 W and exactly a quarter of the supplied energy is lost. The block has mass 0.75 kg. Find its specific heat capacity.
questions.explanation: The block receives 80 × 90 × 3/4 = 5400 J. The mass–temperature product is 9 kg °C, so its heat capacity per kg is 600.

questions.stem: Which quantity differs between neutral atoms of two isotopes of the same element?
questions.explanation: Isotopes have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Neutral atoms then have the same number of electrons.

questions.stem: An ideal transformer converts 30 V to 120 V. If its primary draws 4 A, how much current does its secondary deliver?
questions.explanation: The voltage rises fourfold, so the current falls fourfold at fixed transferred power.

questions.stem: A sound source moving directly towards a listener emits a steady note. It passes the listener and travels directly away. How does the heard note change across this event?

options.label: A
options.text: From above the emitted pitch to below it

options.label: B
options.text: From below the emitted pitch to above it

options.label: C
options.text: The pitch stays above the emitted pitch throughout.

options.label: D
options.text: The pitch stays below the emitted pitch throughout.

options.label: E
options.text: The pitch stays exactly at the emitted pitch.

questions.explanation: The motion crowds wavefronts ahead of the source and spreads those behind it. The observed frequency falls from above to below the emitted frequency.

questions.stem: An ideal transformer has 100 input turns and 400 output turns. It receives 6 V and the load draws 0.5 A. Which row gives output voltage; input current?
questions.explanation: The turns ratio multiplies voltage by four. Equal input and output power require input current four times the 0.5 A output.

questions.stem: One decay step lowers atomic number by two. A following step raises it by one, and neither gamma emission nor any other step occurs. Which ordered pair of emissions fits?
questions.explanation: An alpha removes two protons; beta-minus changes a neutron into a proton, increasing atomic number.

questions.stem: A station sends signals using radio waves. Why can the signal travel between a spacecraft and Earth?

options.label: A
options.text: Radio waves carry moving air all the way from Earth.

options.label: B
options.text: Radio waves can propagate through a vacuum.

options.label: C
options.text: Radio waves are a special case of longitudinal sound.

options.label: D
options.text: Radio waves require an electric cable between sender and receiver.

options.label: E
options.text: Radio waves propagate only through dense gases.

questions.explanation: Radio waves are electromagnetic, hence require no material medium.

questions.stem: A source alone gives 160 counts/min. After 18 hours it gives 20 counts/min. Which row gives its half-life (h); count rate after 24 h (counts/min)?
questions.explanation: An eightfold drop is three half-lives, so each lasts 6 h. Another 6 h halves 20 to 10.

questions.stem: A coil beside a stationary magnet is connected to a voltmeter. Moving the coil directly away creates a reading. What explains this?

options.label: A
options.text: The magnet has become an electric cell.

options.label: B
options.text: The wire becomes a permanent magnet.

options.label: C
options.text: The magnetic flux through the coil changes.

options.label: D
options.text: There must have been a constant current when both were still.

questions.explanation: Electromagnetic induction requires a changing magnetic flux. Relative motion can create this even if the magnet itself does not move.

questions.stem: A student sees five complete wave cycles pass a point in 2 seconds. At the same time, the wavelength is 0.4 m. Find the wave speed.
questions.explanation: The frequency is 2.5 Hz. Multiply by 0.4 m to find speed, rather than multiplying by the number of waves alone.

questions.stem: A transmission line has the same resistance throughout a comparison. At fixed transmitted power, send voltage is raised from V to 3V. Initially the cable dissipates 900 W. Find the new loss.
questions.explanation: Tripling voltage cuts current to a third at fixed transmitted power. Resistive loss depends on the square of current, so it drops to one ninth.

questions.stem:
Three elements have atomic numbers 8, 9 and 10. Their most common isotopes have mass numbers 16, 19 and 20, respectively.

What determines the order of these elements in the Periodic Table?

options.label: A
options.text: The number of neutrons in an atom

options.label: B
options.text: The mass number of the most common isotope

options.label: C
options.text: The number of occupied electron shells

options.label: D
options.text: The number of protons in an atom

options.label: E
options.text: The number of electrons in the first shell

options.label: F
options.text: The sum of the protons, neutrons and electrons

questions.explanation: The Periodic Table orders elements by atomic number, which is the proton count. Even if mass numbers happen to increase in the same order in this example, they do not determine the position.

questions.stem:
Atom X has 12 protons and 12 neutrons.

Which atom is a different isotope of the same element as X?
questions.explanation: Isotopes have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. A nucleus with 11 protons and 13 neutrons has the same mass number as X, but belongs to a different element.

questions.stem: Which feature best explains why neon is much less chemically reactive than sodium?

options.label: A
options.text: Neon has a full outer electron shell.

options.label: C
options.text: Neon has only one electron shell.

options.label: D
options.text: Neon has one electron in its outer shell.

options.label: E
options.text: Neon is less reactive because it has more protons than sodium.

options.label: F
options.text: Neon needs to gain one electron to fill its outer shell.

questions.explanation: Neon already has a full outer shell, so it has little tendency to gain, lose or share electrons. One electron in the outer shell describes sodium, not neon.

questions.stem:
Equal-sized pieces of lithium and potassium are compared in a reaction with excess water.

What is true of the more reactive metal and the gas produced?

options.label: A
options.text: Lithium is more reactive; both give hydrogen.

options.label: B
options.text: Potassium is more reactive; both give oxygen.

options.label: C
options.text: Potassium is more reactive; both give hydrogen.

options.label: D
options.text: Lithium is more reactive; both give oxygen.

options.label: E
options.text: Potassium is more reactive; it gives hydrogen but lithium gives oxygen.

options.label: F
options.text: The metals are equally reactive; both give hydrogen.

questions.explanation: Group 1 metals become more reactive down the group, so potassium reacts more vigorously. Both metals form hydroxides and release hydrogen; the different rates do not imply different gases.

questions.stem:
Oxygen and aluminium have atomic numbers 8 and 13, respectively.

How many electrons are there in one O²⁻ ion and one Al³⁺ ion, respectively?
questions.explanation: Oxygen gains two electrons to form O²⁻, while aluminium loses three to form Al³⁺. Both then have ten electrons; a positive ion has lost electrons, not gained them.

questions.stem:
Solid carbon dioxide sublimes at a much lower temperature than is needed to break up the lattice of diamond.

Which statement explains this difference?

options.label: A
options.text: Carbon dioxide molecules contain only weak covalent bonds, whereas diamond contains strong ones.

options.label: B
options.text: Diamond contains strong ionic bonds; carbon dioxide does not.

options.label: C
options.text: Only intermolecular forces are overcome in diamond, and they are weaker in carbon dioxide.

options.label: D
options.text: Diamond has large molecules held together by ionic bonds.

options.label: E
options.text: Many strong covalent bonds must be broken in diamond, but only intermolecular forces are overcome when solid carbon dioxide sublimes.

options.label: F
options.text: The molecules in solid carbon dioxide are held together by metallic bonds.

questions.explanation: Diamond is a giant covalent network, while solid carbon dioxide consists of separate molecules. Sublimation separates those molecules without breaking their strong C=O bonds.

questions.stem:
Iron is extracted from its oxide in the reaction Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂.

Which statement describes the change to the iron compound?

options.label: A
options.text: It is oxidised because it loses oxygen.

options.label: B
options.text: It is reduced because it gains oxygen.

options.label: C
options.text: It is oxidised because iron changes from +3 to 0.

options.label: D
options.text: It is neither oxidised nor reduced because the oxygen atoms are conserved.

options.label: E
options.text: It is reduced because it loses oxygen.

options.label: F
options.text: It is reduced because it loses electrons.

questions.explanation: The iron oxide loses oxygen and is reduced to iron. The oxygen atoms are still present in carbon dioxide, but atom conservation does not rule out redox.

questions.stem:
A compound contains only the ions T³⁺ and U²⁻. An identical set of ions occurs 12 times in a sample, each set being the smallest electrically neutral combination.

How many U²⁻ ions are in the sample?
questions.explanation: Two T³⁺ ions give +6 and three U²⁻ ions give −6. There are therefore 3 × 12 = 36 anions; the charge on an individual ion is not its count in a formula unit.

questions.stem:
Element J has electron configuration 2,8,2 and element K has electron configuration 2,7. J and K form an ionic compound in which both ions have full outer shells.

How many electrons are present in one formula unit of the compound?
questions.explanation: J loses two electrons to become J²⁺ and each K gains one to become K⁻. The formula is JK₂, with 10 electrons per ion, so there are 30 electrons; counting only one ion of each would give 20.

questions.stem:
Transition metal X forms XO and X₂O₃. Oxygen has oxidation state −2 in both.

For equal numbers of X atoms, what is the ratio of oxygen atoms in XO to those in X₂O₃, and how does X’s oxidation state change from XO to X₂O₃?
questions.explanation: Two XO units and one X₂O₃ unit each contain two metal atoms, but have two and three oxygen atoms respectively. Balancing the oxygen oxidation states gives +2 then +3 for X; comparing one unit of each would not use equal numbers of X atoms.

questions.stem:
What is the relative formula mass of magnesium phosphate, Mg₃(PO₄)₂?

Relative atomic masses: Mg = 24, P = 31, O = 16.
questions.explanation: There are three Mg, two P and eight O atoms per formula unit, so the relative formula mass is 72 + 62 + 128 = 262. The outer 2 multiplies everything inside the parentheses.

questions.stem: A student adds excess zinc to dilute hydrochloric acid. After removing the unreacted zinc, which salt remains in solution?
questions.explanation: A metal reacting with hydrochloric acid forms a chloride salt and hydrogen. Removing the leftover metal does not remove the dissolved zinc chloride.

questions.stem:
At the temperature and pressure used, one mole of gas occupies 24 dm³.

How many moles are in 360 cm³ of gas?
questions.explanation: Convert 360 cm³ to 0.360 dm³ and divide by 24 dm³/mol. Dividing 360 directly by 24 mixes cubic centimetres and cubic decimetres.

questions.stem:
A 50 cm³ sample of a 0.40 mol/dm³ sodium chloride solution is mixed with 150 cm³ of a 0.20 mol/dm³ sodium chloride solution. Assume the volumes add.

What is the resulting concentration?
questions.explanation: The solutions contribute 0.020 and 0.030 mol, giving 0.050 mol in 0.200 dm³. That is 0.25 mol/dm³; taking the simple mean ignores the unequal volumes.

questions.stem:
A hot saturated solution contains 48 g of a salt per 100 g of water. It is cooled without losing water until the solubility is 20 g per 100 g of water.

How much salt crystallises if the solution contains 150 g of water?
questions.explanation: In 150 g of water there are initially 72 g of dissolved salt and finally 30 g, so 42 g crystallises. The 28 g difference in the stated solubilities is per 100 g of water, not per 150 g.

questions.stem:
Acid solution A has pH 3 and acid solution B has pH 5.

What is the ratio of the hydrogen ion concentration in A to that in B?
questions.explanation: A drop of one pH unit means ten times the hydrogen ion concentration. A is two units lower, so its concentration is 100 times B’s; the higher pH is the less acidic solution.

questions.stem:
A mixture contains 0.20 mol of CO and 0.30 mol of CO₂.

Which fraction of the total mass is oxygen?

Relative atomic masses: C = 12, O = 16.
questions.explanation: There are 0.50 mol of carbon atoms and 0.80 mol of oxygen atoms, with masses 6.0 g and 12.8 g respectively. The mass fraction is 12.8/18.8 = 32/47; the fraction of atoms that are oxygen is not the mass fraction.

questions.stem:
Iron reacts with sulfur: Fe + S → FeS. A mixture of 14.0 g of iron and 6.4 g of sulfur reacts as completely as possible.

What total mass of solid is left, excluding the iron sulfide?

Relative atomic masses: Fe = 56, S = 32.
questions.explanation: The starting amounts are 0.25 mol Fe and 0.20 mol S. Sulfur limits the 1 : 1 reaction, leaving 0.05 mol of iron, or 2.8 g; a 1 : 1 mole ratio does not imply equal reacting masses.

questions.stem:
A 10 cm³ sample of nitric acid is diluted to 100 cm³. A 40 cm³ portion of the diluted acid is exactly neutralised by 15 cm³ of 0.016 mol/dm³ calcium hydroxide solution.

What was the nitric acid concentration before dilution?
questions.explanation: One mole of Ca(OH)₂ neutralises two moles of HNO₃, so the 40 cm³ portion contains 2 × 0.015 × 0.016 = 0.00048 mol of acid. This is 0.012 mol/dm³ after dilution, so the original concentration was ten times higher, 0.12 mol/dm³; using a 1 : 1 mole ratio would halve the answer.

questions.stem:
Magnesium carbonate decomposes: MgCO₃ → MgO + CO₂. When 16.8 g of magnesium carbonate is used, 6.0 g of magnesium oxide is collected.

What is the percentage yield of magnesium oxide?

Relative atomic masses: Mg = 24, C = 12, O = 16.
questions.explanation: The 16.8 g sample is 0.20 mol of MgCO₃, so the theoretical yield is 0.20 × 40 = 8.0 g of MgO. The yield is 6.0/8.0 = 75%; the starting carbonate mass is not the theoretical oxide yield.

questions.stem: Which state-symbol change represents solid sodium chloride dissolving in water?
questions.explanation: Solid is (s) and dissolved in water is (aq), so NaCl(s) → NaCl(aq) is the correct representation. The symbol (l) would mean liquid sodium chloride itself, not its solution.

questions.stem: A reusable heat pack warms the water surrounding it in an insulated beaker. An identical unactivated pack in a second beaker produces no temperature change. Which energy transfer explains the difference?

options.label: A
options.text: From the activated pack to the water.

options.label: B
options.text: From the water to the activated pack.

options.label: C
options.text: From the activated pack to the water and an equal amount back to the pack.

options.label: D
options.text: From the unactivated pack to its water.

options.label: E
options.text: From both samples of water into their packs.

options.label: F
options.text: There is no net transfer of energy between either pack and its water.

questions.explanation: Only the water surrounding the activated pack warms. Energy passes from the activated pack to its surroundings.

questions.stem: Why is direct current used rather than alternating current to maintain steady deposition of a metal at one electrode?

options.label: B
options.text: It makes the metal ions negatively charged.

options.label: C
options.text: It reverses the electrodes at regular intervals.

options.label: D
options.text: It keeps the same electrode negative.

options.label: E
options.text: It prevents ions from moving in the electrolyte.

options.label: F
options.text: It removes the need for an electrolyte.

questions.explanation: The negative electrode attracts metal cations and supplies electrons, so holding it negative keeps deposition at the same electrode. Alternating current reverses the electrode polarities.

questions.stem:
In a closed vessel, CO(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO₂(g) + H₂(g). Raising the temperature decreases the amount of CO₂ at equilibrium.

What is the sign of ΔH for the forward reaction, and what would decreasing the volume at constant temperature do to the position of equilibrium?
questions.explanation: Heating favours the reverse direction, so the forward reaction is exothermic and ΔH is negative. Compression would favour the side with fewer moles of gas, but there are two on each side, so there is no shift.

questions.stem:
A lump of an insoluble solid reacts with a solution. The experiment is repeated with the same mass of solid powdered instead, keeping the solution concentration and temperature fixed.

Why is the initial rate higher with the powder?

options.label: A
options.text: More surface is exposed, giving more collisions per second between the reactants.

options.label: B
options.text: Particles in the powder have higher average kinetic energy.

options.label: C
options.text: The powder lowers the reaction’s activation energy.

options.label: D
options.text: The powder increases the total number of solid particles at the atomic level.

options.label: E
options.text: The powder increases the solution’s concentration.

options.label: F
options.text: The powder increases the energy of each collision.

questions.explanation: Powdering exposes more of the solid to the solution, so more collisions can occur each second. It does not itself raise the temperature or lower the activation barrier.

questions.stem:
A reaction produces 12 cm³ of gas by 10 s and 21 cm³ by 25 s.

What is the average rate of gas production between 10 and 25 s?
questions.explanation: The volume increases by 9 cm³ in the 15 s interval, so the average rate is 0.60 cm³/s. Dividing 21 by 25 gives the average from the start, not for this interval.

questions.stem: In the ionic reaction 2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂, which species acts as the reducing agent?
questions.explanation: Iodide loses electrons to form iodine, so it is oxidised and reduces Fe³⁺. Fe³⁺ accepts the electrons and is the oxidising agent, not the reducing agent.

questions.stem:
The uncatalysed forward activation energy of a reversible reaction is 90 kJ/mol. The products are 20 kJ/mol above the reactants. A catalyst lowers the forward activation energy to 55 kJ/mol without changing the product or reactant energies.

What are the uncatalysed and catalysed activation energies, respectively, for the reverse reaction?
questions.explanation: The reverse reaction starts at the products, 20 kJ/mol above the reactants. The two peaks are 90 and 55 kJ/mol above the reactants, so the reverse barriers are 90 − 20 = 70 and 55 − 20 = 35 kJ/mol; the catalyst changes the peak, not the starting energy.

questions.stem:
Ethene reacts with hydrogen: C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆. Use these mean bond energies, in kJ/mol: C=C 610, C–C 350, H–H 440, C–H 410.

What is the estimated enthalpy change per mole of ethene?
questions.explanation: The changed bonds are one C=C and one H–H broken, and one C–C and two C–H formed. The estimate is 610 + 440 − 350 − 2 × 410 = −120 kJ/mol; counting only one new C–H bond misses one added hydrogen.

questions.stem:
During electrolysis of molten magnesium chloride, the electrode products are magnesium metal and chlorine gas. Assume no side reactions.

Which pair gives the moles of magnesium atoms and chlorine molecules produced, respectively, when 0.60 mol of electrons passes through the external circuit?
questions.explanation: Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Mg uses two electrons per metal atom, and 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ releases two per chlorine molecule. Both amounts are 0.60/2 = 0.30 mol; the number of chlorine atoms would be twice the number of molecules.

questions.stem: What changes when pure liquid water freezes at its freezing point?

options.label: B
options.text: The molecules move freely past one another more easily.

options.label: C
options.text: The molecules become fixed in position but continue to vibrate.

options.label: E
options.text: The molecules split into hydrogen and oxygen atoms.

options.label: F
options.text: The arrangement becomes less ordered and the molecules move much farther apart.

questions.explanation: In ice, the molecules vibrate about fixed positions instead of moving past one another as they do in a liquid. Freezing changes their arrangement and motion, not the identity of the molecules.

questions.stem: Why is chlorine added in controlled amounts during drinking-water treatment?

options.label: B
options.text: To supply fluoride for dental health

options.label: F
options.text: To soften the water by removing calcium ions

questions.explanation: Chlorine disinfects water by killing harmful microorganisms. Fluoride, where used, has a different purpose and does not explain chlorination.

questions.stem:
A salt containing just one type of metal ion gives a lilac flame in a flame test.

Which metal ion is indicated?
questions.explanation: Potassium gives a lilac flame. Sodium gives a yellow-orange flame, so a lilac colour does not indicate sodium.

questions.stem:
A mixture contains an insoluble solid and dissolved salt in water. A student wants to recover both solids separately, without needing to collect the water.

Which sequence works?

options.label: B
options.text: Crystallise first, then filter out both solids together.

options.label: C
options.text: Decant once, then dry what remains without further separation.

options.label: E
options.text: Use a separating funnel, then evaporate the lower layer.

options.label: F
options.text: Centrifuge once, then dry only the pellet.

questions.explanation: Filtration collects the insoluble solid as the residue. The dissolved salt passes into the filtrate, which can then be concentrated and crystallised; it will not be recovered by drying the residue alone.

questions.stem:
Hex-2-ene reacts with enough hydrogen to add across its carbon–carbon double bond. No carbon atoms are lost.

What is the product?
questions.explanation: Adding H₂ makes the double bond single and adds two H atoms to C₆H₁₂, giving C₆H₁₄. Hydrogenation neither shifts the double bond nor introduces oxygen.

questions.stem: What is the correct name of the alcohol CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₂CH₂CH₃?
questions.explanation: The longest chain has six carbon atoms, and numbering from the nearer end puts OH at carbon 3. Numbering from the other end gives 4, but the lower locant must be used.

questions.stem:
Two colourless solutions contain different sodium halides. After acidification with dilute nitric acid and addition of aqueous silver nitrate, solution X gives a cream precipitate and Y gives a yellow precipitate.

Which halides are present in X and Y, respectively?
questions.explanation: Silver bromide is cream and silver iodide is yellow. Chloride would form a white precipitate, so it cannot account for either observation.

questions.stem:
On a chromatogram, the baseline is 10 mm from the bottom edge of the paper and the solvent front is 70 mm from that edge. A reference dye has an Rf of 0.60 in this solvent.

How far from the bottom edge would a spot with the same Rf be?
questions.explanation: The solvent travelled 60 mm from the baseline, so the spot travelled 0.60 × 60 = 36 mm from the same line. Add the 10 mm baseline offset; 36 mm is not the distance from the bottom edge.

questions.stem:
Propane burns in limited oxygen and produces carbon monoxide and water as its only products. The equation is balanced using the smallest whole-number coefficients.

What is the sum of all four coefficients?
questions.explanation: First write C₃H₈ + ⁷⁄₂O₂ → 3CO + 4H₂O, then double all coefficients to give 2, 7, 6 and 8, whose sum is 23. Treating the carbon product as CO₂ would require more oxygen.

questions.stem:
Propanoic acid, C₂H₅COOH, reacts with solid MgCO₃ to give a magnesium salt, carbon dioxide and water. The reaction produces 0.050 mol of carbon dioxide.

What mass of the magnesium salt forms?

Relative atomic masses: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16, Mg = 24.
questions.explanation: The salt is Mg(C₂H₅COO)₂, with relative formula mass 24 + 2 × 73 = 170. Each mole of carbonate gives one mole of CO₂ and one mole of the salt, so 0.050 × 170 = 8.5 g; the 2 : 1 acid-to-salt ratio is not the CO₂-to-salt ratio.

questions.stem: The ground-state electron arrangement of a neutral silicon atom is 2,8,4. A student labels a diagram as showing the outer shell. How many electrons should be shown in that shell?
questions.explanation: The last number in 2,8,4 is the number of electrons in the outer shell.

questions.stem: A main-group atom has electron arrangement 2,8,7. What is its period?
questions.explanation: Three shells are occupied. The seven outer electrons relate to the group rather than the period.

questions.stem: Why does pure solid sodium chloride not conduct electricity?

options.label: B
options.text: Its electrons carry a net positive charge.

options.label: C
options.text: The sodium and chloride are neutral atoms.

questions.explanation: The ions are fixed in the solid lattice. When molten, the ions can move and carry charge without becoming neutral.

questions.stem:
Two neutral magnesium isotopes are ²⁴Mg and ²⁶Mg, both with atomic number 12. Which statements are correct?

1. Both have twelve electrons.

2. The heavier isotope has two more protons.

3. The heavier isotope has fourteen neutrons.
questions.explanation: The atomic number fixes proton number at 12 and hence the neutral electron count. Neutrons in ²⁶Mg number 26 − 12.

questions.stem: Which property is shared by atoms of neon and argon in their ground states?

options.label: A
options.text: They have the same number of occupied shells.

options.label: B
options.text: They each have two outer electrons.

options.label: C
options.text: They have the same atomic number.

questions.explanation: Both are noble gases with filled outer shells. Being in the same group does not give them the same number of occupied shells.

questions.stem: A compound contains only Ca²⁺ and PO₄³⁻ ions. Which row gives the numbers of calcium ions; phosphate ions in its simplest formula unit?
questions.explanation: The smallest equal charge totals are +6 and −6, requiring three calcium and two phosphate ions. Subscripts do not equal the corresponding charge magnitudes directly.

questions.stem: Which particles primarily carry charge through a solid copper wire?

options.label: C
options.text: Copper ions moving along the wire

questions.explanation: Delocalised electrons can move through the metal. Copper ions remain in the lattice and do not drift along the wire.

questions.stem: An element contains only isotopes of mass numbers 63 and 65. Its relative atomic mass is 63.6. What percentage of atoms are the heavier isotope?
questions.explanation: Replacing a light atom with a heavy one adds 2 mass units. The average excess of 0.6 therefore corresponds to 0.6/2 of the atoms.

questions.stem: Ion X has 12 protons and 10 electrons. Ion Y has 17 protons and 18 electrons. Which row gives the formula of their neutral compound; total electrons per formula unit?
questions.explanation: X is 2+ and Y is 1−, so two Y ions accompany each X ion. Count their actual electrons: 10 + 2 × 18.

questions.stem: Equal freshly cut pieces of sodium and lithium are placed separately in water at the same temperature. Which observation best supports the expected reactivity trend?

options.label: C
options.text: Sodium reacts but lithium never reacts.

options.label: F
options.text: Both react only if the water is boiling.

questions.explanation: Group 1 metals become more reactive down the group. Sodium lies below lithium, so it is expected to react more vigorously.

questions.stem: A label shows the formula X₂O₃ and a relative formula mass of 160. Given Aᵣ(O) = 16, what is Aᵣ(X)?
questions.explanation: The three oxygen atoms contribute 48. The two X atoms contribute 160 − 48 = 112, so each contributes 56.

questions.stem: How many moles are in 9 g of water? Use Aᵣ(H) = 1 and Aᵣ(O) = 16.
questions.explanation: Water has molar mass 18 g/mol. Divide the given mass by 18; do not use 16 for the whole molecule.

questions.stem: A solution contains 0.06 mol of solute in 200 cm³. Find the concentration in mol/dm³.
questions.explanation: 200 cm³ is 0.200 dm³, giving 0.06/0.200 = 0.30 mol/dm³. Using 200 directly mixes units.

questions.stem: In 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, 0.30 mol Mg reacts with 0.20 mol O₂. Which row gives MgO formed; O₂ left (both in mol)?
questions.explanation: The magnesium needs 0.15 mol oxygen, so magnesium limits production to 0.30 mol MgO. The unused oxygen is 0.05 mol.

questions.stem: Complete CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + X(g). Which formula balances the equation?
questions.explanation: Removing CaO from the formula leaves one carbon and two oxygens. Coefficients and subscripts cannot be interchanged.

questions.stem: Gas A occupies 3.6 dm³ at conditions where each mole occupies 24 dm³. Which row gives amount (mol); volume of twice that amount (cm³)?
questions.explanation: Divide 3.6 by 24 for moles. Twice the amount occupies 7.2 dm³, and each dm³ is 1000 cm³.

questions.stem: A calculation predicts 32 g of product but the isolated mass is 24 g. What is the percentage yield?
questions.explanation: Percentage yield is actual divided by theoretical times 100. The 25% is the shortfall, not the yield.

questions.stem: 25.0 cm³ of a solution of H₂SO₄ requires 30.0 cm³ of 0.20 mol/dm³ NaOH for complete neutralisation. Find the acid concentration in mol/dm³.
questions.explanation: The alkali provides 0.006 mol NaOH. Two moles of NaOH neutralise one mole of H₂SO₄, so 0.003 mol acid in 0.025 dm³ gives 0.12 mol/dm³.

questions.stem: A 300 cm³ solution contains 0.40 mol/dm³ solute. A 50 cm³ aliquot is removed and diluted to 200 cm³. Which row gives the solute remaining in the original vessel (mol); diluted aliquot concentration (mol/dm³)?
questions.explanation: After removal, 250 cm³ at 0.40 mol/dm³ holds 0.10 mol. The removed 0.02 mol ends up in 0.20 dm³, hence 0.10 mol/dm³.

questions.stem: A sample contains only magnesium carbonate and inert solid. Heating 21 g leaves 14.4 g of residue after all CO₂ escapes. What mass percentage was MgCO₃? Use Aᵣ(Mg) = 24, Aᵣ(C) = 12, Aᵣ(O) = 16.
questions.explanation: The 6.6 g loss is CO₂, or 0.15 mol. Equal moles of MgCO₃ were present, giving 12.6 g out of 21 g; the lost mass is not the carbonate mass.

questions.stem: A class compares how quickly whole and crushed chalk react with excess acid. They intend to vary the surface area of the chalk only. Which pair of trials gives a fair comparison?

options.label: A
options.text: 5 g whole and 5 g crushed, with the same acid volume, concentration and temperature.

options.label: B
options.text: 5 g whole and 10 g crushed, with the same acid conditions.

options.label: C
options.text: 5 g whole and 5 g crushed, with twice the acid concentration in the crushed trial.

options.label: D
options.text: 5 g whole and 5 g crushed, with warmer acid in the whole trial.

options.label: E
options.text: 5 g whole and 5 g crushed, with twice the acid volume in the whole trial.

questions.explanation: Equal masses of the same material and identical acid conditions isolate the effect of changing the particle size, and hence the exposed surface area.

questions.stem: A dissolving process makes a well-insulated beaker noticeably colder. How should the process be classified?
questions.explanation: The dissolving process absorbs energy from its surroundings, cooling them. Cooling of the surroundings does not mean the process gives energy out.

questions.stem: In Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, which species loses electrons?
questions.explanation: Zn forms Zn²⁺ by losing two electrons. Cu²⁺ gains electrons, so it is reduced rather than oxidised.

questions.stem:
A gas syringe reads 0, 18, 30 and 36 cm³ at 0, 6, 12 and 18 s. Which statements are correct?

1. Mean rate over the whole record is 2 cm³/s.

2. Mean rate over the first 6 s is 3 cm³/s.

3. Mean rate over the last 6 s is 2 cm³/s.
questions.explanation: The first and last intervals give 18/6 and 6/6. Across all 18 s the increase is 36 cm³, so the average is 2 cm³/s.

questions.stem: In N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), the mixture at equilibrium is compressed at constant temperature. Which direction is favoured?

options.label: B
options.text: Neither, because both sides contain gas

questions.explanation: The product side has fewer gas molecules per reaction event. Compression favours that side, not the one with more different gases.

questions.stem: The energy levels of reactants, transition state and products are 50, 120 and 30 kJ/mol. Which row gives forward activation energy; forward enthalpy change (kJ/mol)?
questions.explanation: Activation energy is transition state minus reactants, 70. Enthalpy change is products minus reactants, −20, not the drop from the transition state.

questions.stem: Molten lead bromide is electrolysed with inert electrodes. Which species is reduced?
questions.explanation: Lead ions gain electrons at the cathode. Bromide loses electrons at the anode.

questions.stem: Use bond energies in kJ/mol: H–H 436, Cl–Cl 242, H–Cl 431. For H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl, find the estimated enthalpy change in kJ/mol.
questions.explanation: Breaking H–H and Cl–Cl costs 678 kJ/mol. Forming two H–Cl bonds releases 862 kJ/mol, so net change is −184; count both product bonds.

questions.stem: A reaction has an uncatalysed forward barrier of 105 kJ/mol and forward enthalpy change +35 kJ/mol. A catalyst lowers the forward barrier by 25 kJ/mol. Which row gives the catalysed forward; reverse barriers (kJ/mol)?
questions.explanation: The catalyst lowers the forward barrier to 80. Products lie 35 above reactants, so the reverse barrier to the same transition state is 80 − 35.

questions.stem: A mixture warms 100 g of solution by 6 °C. Specific heat capacity is 4.2 J/(g °C); ignore the cup. If 0.030 mol reacted, what heat was released per mole?
questions.explanation: The solution absorbs 100 × 4.2 × 6 = 2520 J. Divide by 0.030 mol and convert J to kJ; 2.52 kJ is the heat for the sample only.

questions.stem: A hydrocarbon molecule has four carbon atoms in an open chain. All its bonds are single except for one carbon–carbon double bond. How many hydrogen atoms does it contain?
questions.explanation: An open-chain alkane with four carbon atoms has ten hydrogens. One carbon–carbon double bond reduces the number by two, to eight.

questions.stem: Which ion gives a yellow flame in a standard flame test?
questions.explanation: Sodium gives yellow, whereas lithium gives crimson and potassium gives lilac. Flame colours are specific to the metal ion, not the accompanying anion.

questions.stem: Which technique recovers water, rather than the dissolved salt, from salt water?
questions.explanation: Vaporise the water and condense it elsewhere. Evaporation alone does not collect the water.

questions.stem:
Consider complete combustion of one molecule of butane, C₄H₁₀. Which statements are correct?

1. Four CO₂ molecules form per butane molecule.

2. Five H₂O molecules form per butane molecule.

3. Nine O₂ molecules are needed per butane molecule.
questions.explanation: Conserving C and H gives four CO₂ and five H₂O, containing 13 oxygen atoms in total. That requires 6.5 O₂ per butane on average, not nine.

questions.stem: Acidified silver nitrate produces a cream precipitate in a sample known to contain one type of halide ion. Which halide is it?
questions.explanation: Silver bromide gives a cream precipitate; silver chloride gives white and silver iodide yellow. The test distinguishes these colours rather than presence of any precipitate alone.

questions.stem: On one chromatogram the solvent travels 8 cm. Two spots travel 2 cm and 6 cm. Which row gives the Rf values for the nearer; farther spot?
questions.explanation: Divide each spot distance by the solvent distance from the baseline. Do not divide one spot distance by the other.

questions.stem: Which compound has the same molecular formula as propan-1-ol but a different arrangement of atoms?
questions.explanation: Moving the OH group from carbon 1 to carbon 2 leaves C₃H₈O unchanged. Propanone has two fewer hydrogen atoms.

questions.stem: Ethanoic acid reacts with sodium hydrogencarbonate. Which row names the salt; the gaseous product?
questions.explanation: The acid loses its acidic H to form ethanoate. Hydrogencarbonate produces carbon dioxide and water, not the hydrogen associated with some acid–metal reactions.

questions.stem: 0.15 mol of an unknown hydrocarbon adds 0.30 mol H₂ to its carbon–carbon double bonds to give a saturated acyclic product. The carbon skeleton remains intact. How many C=C bonds did each molecule have?
questions.explanation: Each C=C consumes one H₂, so the ratio 0.30/0.15 counts two double bonds. Each H₂ supplies two atoms, but that does not double the bond count.

questions.stem: A treatment plant has removed suspended particles, but harmful microorganisms may remain. What is the purpose of the disinfection stage?

options.label: C
options.text: To increase the volume of water

options.label: D
options.text: To add suspended particles for filtration

questions.explanation: Disinfection reduces the risk from microorganisms. Removing suspended solids or dissolved salts is a distinct treatment goal.

questions.stem: In order of increasing atomic number, element X comes immediately after the last element in period 3. Use group numbers 1–18. Where is X in the periodic table?
questions.explanation: After the last element of period 3, the next electron goes into a new outer shell. That puts X at the start of period 4, in group 1.

questions.stem: An ion with charge 2+ has 18 electrons. How many electrons are in the outer shell of its neutral atom?
questions.explanation: The neutral atom has 20 electrons, arranged 2,8,8,2. Do not use the outer shell of the ion.

questions.stem: Why does graphite conduct along its layers but diamond does not conduct?

options.label: C
options.text: Graphite has mobile electrons; diamond does not.

options.label: D
options.text: Graphite has metallic bonds between all carbon atoms.

options.label: E
options.text: Diamond conducts only through its outer atoms.

questions.explanation: Graphite has delocalised electrons in its layers. Diamond uses its outer electrons in covalent bonds and lacks mobile charge carriers.

questions.stem: Two isotopes have masses 10 and 11. In 50 atoms, 12 are the lighter isotope. Which row gives the percentage heavier; mean mass number?
questions.explanation: There are 38 heavier atoms. Their share is 76%; each adds one unit relative to a mass-10 baseline.

questions.stem: Separate solutions contain 0.2 mol Mg²⁺ ions and 0.3 mol PO₄³⁻ ions. Solid Mg₃(PO₄)₂ forms as far as possible. Which ion is left in excess?
questions.explanation: The 3:2 formula means 0.2 mol magnesium needs only 0.2 × 2/3 mol phosphate. The phosphate is in excess.

questions.stem: Chlorine water is added separately to bromide and chloride solutions. Which results occur, considering halogen displacement only?

options.label: D
options.text: Bromine forms in the bromide solution; no displacement of chloride.

options.label: E
options.text: Bromine forms in the chloride solution only.

questions.explanation: Chlorine is more reactive than bromine and can oxidise bromide. A halogen does not displace itself from its own halide.

questions.stem: Two pure substances have similar molecular masses; one is ionic and one is simple molecular. Which usually has the higher melting point and why?

options.label: A
options.text: The ionic substance, because of strong electrostatic attractions between ions.

options.label: B
options.text: The molecular substance, because melting breaks its internal covalent bonds.

options.label: C
options.text: The ionic substance, because its ions have no charge.

options.label: D
options.text: Both must melt at the same temperature.

options.label: E
options.text: The molecular substance, because similar masses imply strongest bonding.

questions.explanation: Melting an ionic solid disrupts strong attractions across the lattice. A simple molecular solid usually melts when weaker intermolecular forces are overcome.

questions.stem: An element has isotopes 28, 29 and 30. The fraction of 29 is twice that of 30, and the mean mass is 28.4. Which row gives the percentages of 28; 29; 30?
questions.explanation: If fraction x is mass-30, the mean excess over 28 is 2x + 2x. Thus x = 0.1 and the other fractions are 0.2 and 0.7.

questions.stem: Ions X²⁺ and Y⁻ contain 10 and 18 electrons, respectively. Which row gives the proton counts of their neutral atoms (X; Y)?
questions.explanation: X lost two electrons and Y gained one, so the neutral counts are 12 and 17. Ion formation changes electrons, not protons.

questions.stem: Solid X conducts; molten X also conducts. Solid Y is insulating but molten Y conducts. Which assignment best explains both observations?
questions.explanation: Mobile electrons can conduct in a metal in both states. Ions in Y become mobile only when molten.

questions.stem: A technician needs the same number of formula units in samples of sodium chloride and magnesium oxide. The sodium chloride sample has mass 117 g. The relative formula masses are 58.5 and 40 respectively. What mass of magnesium oxide is needed?
questions.explanation: There are 117 ÷ 58.5 = 2 mol of sodium chloride. Equal numbers of formula units require equal amounts in moles, so use 2 × 40 = 80 g of magnesium oxide.

questions.stem: An oxide contains 27 g of aluminium and 24 g of oxygen. Find its empirical formula. Use Aᵣ(Al)=27 and Aᵣ(O)=16.
questions.explanation: The amounts are 1 mol Al and 1.5 mol O. Double the ratio to use whole-number subscripts.

questions.stem: Find the percentage by mass of carbon in carbon dioxide. Use Aᵣ(C)=12 and Aᵣ(O)=16.
questions.explanation: Carbon contributes 12 out of 44 mass units. Multiply 12/44 by 100, not by 100 twice.

questions.stem: At fixed temperature and pressure, a gas mixture contains 2 dm³ of A and 6 dm³ of B. Which row gives mole fraction of A; moles of B if the molar volume is 24 dm³?
questions.explanation: At fixed conditions mole shares equal volume shares. A takes 2/8 of the volume; B contains 6/24 mol.

questions.stem: Mix 100 cm³ of 0.30 mol/dm³ solution with 100 cm³ of 0.10 mol/dm³ solution of the same solute. Evaporate 50 cm³ of solvent only. What is the final concentration?
questions.explanation: The two solutions supply 0.04 mol in total. Evaporation leaves that amount in 0.15 dm³, not 0.20 dm³.

questions.stem: For 2CO + O₂ → 2CO₂, start with 0.5 mol CO and 0.4 mol O₂. Which row gives moles of CO₂ formed; O₂ left?
questions.explanation: The CO needs 0.25 mol oxygen, leaving 0.15 mol. Equal coefficients mean 0.5 mol CO₂ forms from 0.5 mol CO.

questions.stem: A process makes 18 g of solid with a 60% yield. What mass would a perfect yield give?
questions.explanation: The 18 g is 0.6 times the theoretical mass. Divide by 0.6; multiplying gives a smaller number.

questions.stem: A 25 cm³ portion of vinegar uses 20 cm³ of 0.15 mol/dm³ NaOH. The acid reacts 1:1 and the vinegar was first diluted to one fifth of its original concentration. Find the original acid concentration.
questions.explanation: The diluted sample has 0.003 mol in 0.025 dm³, giving 0.12 mol/dm³. Multiply by five to undo dilution.

questions.stem: A 10 g mixture contains only CaCO₃ and silica. Complete decomposition releases 2.2 g of CO₂. Which row gives CaCO₃ amount (mol); percentage by mass? Use Aᵣ(Ca)=40, Aᵣ(C)=12 and Aᵣ(O)=16.
questions.explanation: Each mole of CaCO₃ gives a mole of CO₂. Thus 2.2/44 = 0.05 mol CaCO₃ weighs 5 g, half the mixture.

questions.stem: An oxide of nitrogen contains 30.4% nitrogen by mass to the nearest 0.1%. Its relative molecular mass is 92. Find its formula. Use Aᵣ(N)=14 and Aᵣ(O)=16.
questions.explanation: One mole contains about 28 g nitrogen and 64 g oxygen. Dividing by each atomic mass yields two nitrogen and four oxygen atoms.

questions.stem: In a sealed container a coloured reactant forms a colourless product in a reversible reaction. After a time, the colour intensity stops changing. The measured concentrations of reactant and product are both nonzero and unequal, and both reactions are still occurring. Which statement describes this state?

options.label: A
options.text: The forward rate must be larger if there is more reactant.

options.label: B
options.text: The rates are equal although the concentrations are unequal.

options.label: C
options.text: The reverse rate must be larger if there is more product.

options.label: D
options.text: The concentrations must become equal before the rates can match.

options.label: E
options.text: The rates alternate between zero and a positive value.

questions.explanation: A constant colour intensity here reflects constant composition. Continued interconversion at constant composition means the forward and reverse rates are equal, not that the concentrations are equal.

questions.stem: A catalyst is added to a system already at equilibrium. What happens to the two rates and the composition?

options.label: A
options.text: Only the forward rate increases; more product forms.

options.label: B
options.text: Both rates decrease; composition stays the same.

options.label: C
options.text: Both rates increase; less product remains.

options.label: D
options.text: Both rates increase; composition stays the same.

options.label: E
options.text: Neither rate changes; more product forms.

questions.explanation: A catalyst lowers barriers in both directions but does not shift equilibrium.

questions.stem: The products on an energy diagram lie 40 kJ/mol above the reactants. What is the forward enthalpy change?
questions.explanation: Enthalpy change is products minus reactants. The higher products make the forward reaction endothermic.

questions.stem: For 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), the forward reaction is exothermic. Which combination favours products most clearly?

options.label: E
options.text: Any combination gives the same position

questions.explanation: Lower temperature favours the exothermic direction. Higher pressure favours fewer gas molecules, also on the product side.

questions.stem: A gas syringe reads 0, 8, 20 and 24 cm³ at 0, 4, 8 and 12 s. Which row gives the fastest four-second mean rate; whole-run mean rate (cm³/s)?
questions.explanation: The increments are 8, 12 and 4 cm³, making the largest interval rate 12/4. The overall rate is 24/12.

questions.stem: Two 50 g solutions of equal specific heat capacity are mixed in an insulated cup, one at 20 °C and one at 40 °C. Their reaction leaves the mixture at 34 °C. If c = 4 J/(g °C), how much heat is released by reaction?
questions.explanation: Without reaction the mixture would be at 30 °C. Raising all 100 g through another 4 °C takes 1600 J.

questions.stem: What does the activation energy of a reaction represent?

options.label: A
options.text: The energy released per mole in every reaction

options.label: B
options.text: The average energy of particles at equilibrium

options.label: C
options.text: The total kinetic energy of the reactants

options.label: D
options.text: The energy of the products only

options.label: E
options.text: The minimum energy needed for a successful collision

questions.explanation: Particles must overcome an energy barrier to react. The activation energy is not the overall energy difference between reactants and products.

questions.stem: The reaction X₂ + Y₂ → 2XY releases 70 kJ/mol. Bond energies X–X and Y–Y are 160 and 230 kJ/mol. Find the mean X–Y bond energy.
questions.explanation: Breaking bonds costs 390 kJ. Forming two new bonds must release 460 kJ to give −70 overall; divide that total by two.

questions.stem: The forward reaction is exothermic by 20 kJ/mol. Before catalysis the reverse activation energy is 80 kJ/mol. A catalyst lowers both activation energies by 15 kJ/mol. Which row gives new forward; reverse barriers?
questions.explanation: The uncatalysed forward barrier is 80 − 20 = 60. Reducing both barriers gives 45 and 65, with the enthalpy difference unchanged.

questions.stem: A reaction raises 80 g of solution from 18 °C to 24 °C. The cup also absorbs 120 J. The solution’s specific heat capacity is 4 J/(g °C), and 0.030 mol reacted. Find heat released per mole.
questions.explanation: The solution absorbs 1920 J and the cup 120 J, for 2040 J total. Divide by 0.030 mol and by 1000.

questions.stem: A student expects a gas to contain carbon dioxide and tests it with fresh limewater. To rule out other causes of cloudiness, the student wants a negative control. Which procedure provides one?

options.label: A
options.text: Bubble the unknown gas through fresh limewater twice.

options.label: B
options.text: Bubble a sample known to be free of carbon dioxide through fresh limewater under the same conditions.

options.label: C
options.text: Bubble a known sample of carbon dioxide through fresh limewater.

options.label: D
options.text: Bubble the unknown gas through pure water instead of limewater.

options.label: E
options.text: Add a second portion of limewater to the cloudy result.

questions.explanation: A matched gas known to lack carbon dioxide should not give the positive test. Testing known carbon dioxide instead is a positive control.

questions.stem: What distinguishes ethanol from ethene at the functional-group level?

options.label: A
options.text: Ethanol has an OH group; ethene has C=C.

options.label: B
options.text: Ethanol has C=C; ethene has OH.

questions.explanation: The alcohol has a hydroxyl group, whereas the alkene contains a carbon–carbon double bond.

questions.stem: A solid mixture contains salt and insoluble sand. What separation step should immediately follow stirring with enough water to dissolve the salt?
questions.explanation: The salt passes through dissolved in water while the sand stays on the filter. Evaporating first would return both solids together.

questions.stem: A spot has Rf = 0.40 in a particular solvent. Two trials have fronts 45 and 75 mm from their baselines. Which row gives the distance of the spot from the baseline in each trial?
questions.explanation: Multiply the solvent distance by Rf in each trial. Use distances from the baseline rather than distances from the paper edge.

questions.stem: Sample A gives a lilac flame and sample B gives a yellow flame. Which row identifies their metal ions (A; B)?
questions.explanation: Lilac identifies potassium and yellow identifies sodium. The flame test identifies these cations, not the counterions.

questions.stem: An open-chain hydrocarbon with six carbon atoms has just one C=C. It adds one mole H₂ per mole of hydrocarbon. Which row gives the molecular formulas before; after addition?
questions.explanation: A single-double-bond acyclic alkene has 2n hydrogens. One H₂ removes the double bond and adds two H atoms.

questions.stem: Which aqueous product accompanies an ester when a carboxylic acid and an alcohol react by esterification?
questions.explanation: Esterification combines the two organic reactants with elimination of water. It is not combustion or carbonate neutralisation.

questions.stem: Complete combustion of 0.20 mol of a hydrocarbon forms 0.80 mol of CO₂ and 1.00 mol of H₂O. Which formula has the required carbon and hydrogen atoms per molecule?
questions.explanation: Per mole of fuel, there are four moles of C in CO₂ and five moles of H₂O, containing ten moles of H atoms.

questions.stem: One salt solution gives a white precipitate with acidified silver nitrate. A different sample of the same solution gives no effervescence with dilute acid. Which anion best fits?
questions.explanation: Silver chloride is white. Bromide and iodide give cream and yellow respectively, and carbonate would produce bubbles with acid.

questions.stem:
In one solvent a sample produces spots at Rf 0.20 and 0.60. A standard gives one spot at 0.60. Which statements are justified?

1. The sample contains at least two components.

2. One is conclusively the standard.

3. Another solvent can help distinguish compounds with the same Rf.
questions.explanation: Two distinct spots require separate components. A matching Rf alone is not conclusive; a different solvent can separate a coincidental match.

questions.stem: In electrolysis, which electrode attracts a cation?
questions.explanation: Cations are positive and move to the negatively charged cathode.

questions.stem: Which salt forms from potassium hydroxide and sulfuric acid alone?
questions.explanation: The base supplies potassium and the acid supplies sulfate. Neutralisation also makes water.

questions.stem: A Cu²⁺ ion becomes a Cu atom. Which change occurs to that ion?
questions.explanation: Two incoming electrons cancel the ion’s +2 charge. This is reduction.

questions.stem: Molten calcium bromide is electrolysed. Which row gives the cathode product; anode product?
questions.explanation: Ca²⁺ is reduced and Br⁻ is oxidised. Hydrogen and oxygen from water are not available in the melt.

questions.stem: For H₂SO₄ + 2KOH → K₂SO₄ + 2H₂O, 0.06 mol acid reacts with 0.10 mol base. How many moles of acid remain?
questions.explanation: The 0.10 mol base consumes half as many moles of acid. Subtract 0.05 from 0.06.

questions.stem: A dilute acid is diluted further with water. What happens to its pH before it becomes indistinguishable from neutral water?
questions.explanation: Adding water reduces hydrogen-ion concentration. An acid becomes less acidic, not alkaline.

questions.stem: A molten salt contains Al³⁺ and Cl⁻. For every 2 mol Al formed, how many moles of electrons pass through the circuit and how many moles of Cl₂ form?
questions.explanation: Each Al³⁺ requires three electrons. Oxidising two Cl⁻ produces one Cl₂ and supplies two electrons, so 6 mol electrons correspond to 3 mol chlorine.

questions.stem: A metal is extracted by reducing its oxide with carbon. What does the extraction method imply about the metal relative to carbon?

options.label: A
options.text: The metal is necessarily more reactive than carbon.

options.label: B
options.text: The metal and carbon must have identical reactivity.

options.label: C
options.text: The metal is necessarily a noble gas.

options.label: D
options.text: The metal is less reactive than carbon.

questions.explanation: Carbon can remove oxygen from the oxide of a less reactive metal. More reactive metals generally require other methods.

questions.stem: A particle changes from an anion of charge 1− to a cation of charge 1+. Which electron transfer could account for this change?
questions.explanation: The charge increases from −1 to +1, a rise of two units. Each lost electron raises the charge by one unit.

questions.stem: A 40 cm³ sample contains only 0.20 mol/dm³ HCl and 0.10 mol/dm³ H₂SO₄. Assume both acid hydrogens in H₂SO₄ are neutralised. Find the volume of 0.40 mol/dm³ NaOH required.
questions.explanation: The total acid equivalents per litre are 0.20 + 2 × 0.10 = 0.40 mol. Equal equivalents per litre require equal volumes.

questions.stem: Why is argon relatively unreactive under ordinary conditions?

options.label: A
options.text: Its outer electron shell is full.

questions.explanation: A filled outer shell makes argon unlikely to gain or lose electrons in ordinary reactions.

questions.stem: An ionic compound contains only Mg²⁺ and N³⁻ ions. A student is drawing one formula unit, using the smallest possible electrically neutral group of these ions. Which group should be drawn?

options.label: A
options.text: Two Mg²⁺ ions and three N³⁻ ions.

options.label: B
