options.text: One Mg²⁺ ion and one N³⁻ ion.

options.label: C
options.text: Three Mg²⁺ ions and one N³⁻ ion.

options.label: D
options.text: One Mg²⁺ ion and two N³⁻ ions.

options.label: E
options.text: Three Mg²⁺ ions and two N³⁻ ions.

options.label: F
options.text: Six Mg²⁺ ions and four N³⁻ ions.

questions.explanation: Three magnesium ions contribute +6 and two nitride ions contribute −6. The larger neutral group duplicates this smallest ratio.

questions.stem: Solid iodine is placed in sodium bromide solution. Does halogen displacement occur at ordinary conditions?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes: iodine is more reactive than bromine.

options.label: B
options.text: No: iodine is less reactive than bromine.

options.label: C
options.text: Yes: sodium is displaced as metal.

options.label: D
options.text: Yes: bromide is reduced to bromine.

options.label: E
options.text: Yes: iodine displaces a more reactive halogen.

questions.explanation: A less reactive halogen cannot displace the halide of a more reactive one. Iodine is below bromine in Group 17.

questions.stem: Two ions, N³⁻ and Mg²⁺, have nuclei with 7 and 12 protons respectively. Which row gives their electron counts (N³⁻; Mg²⁺)?
questions.explanation: The nitride ion gains three electrons and the magnesium ion loses two. Their proton counts stay fixed.

questions.stem: For 2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃, 0.4 mol Al and 0.9 mol Cl₂ react. Find moles of chlorine left.
questions.explanation: The aluminium uses 0.4 × 3/2 = 0.6 mol chlorine. Subtract from 0.9 mol.

questions.stem: A substance consists of discrete polar molecules. Why does melting it not normally break the bonds between atoms inside each molecule?

options.label: A
options.text: Every covalent bond disappears when a solid melts.

options.label: B
options.text: Melting changes the atoms into ions.

options.label: C
options.text: Melting mainly overcomes forces between molecules.

options.label: D
options.text: Intermolecular forces are always stronger than covalent bonds.

options.label: E
options.text: Polar molecules have no internal bonds.

questions.explanation: Breaking interactions between molecules allows them to move past one another; it does not require splitting the molecules.

questions.stem: One complete batch of a reaction makes only 56 g of desired product and 24 g of by-product. At the same reactant ratio, another complete batch starts with 120 g of reactants. Which product masses should it give (desired; by-product)?
questions.explanation: The first batch starts with 80 g by mass conservation. The second is 120/80 times as large, so scale both product masses by 3/2.

questions.stem: Zinc metal is dipped into aqueous copper sulfate and a copper coating forms. What happened to the copper ions?

options.label: B
options.text: They lost electrons to become copper atoms.

options.label: C
options.text: They were unchanged and turned into solid sulfate.

options.label: D
options.text: They gained electrons at the zinc surface.

options.label: E
options.text: They displaced zinc without a charge change.

questions.explanation: Copper ions become neutral copper by gaining electrons. Zinc is the reducing agent and becomes zinc ions.

questions.stem: A liquid evaporates at room temperature without boiling. Where do the escaping molecules leave from?

options.label: B
options.text: Every part of the liquid equally

options.label: C
options.text: Only the bottom of the container

options.label: D
options.text: Only the centre of the liquid

options.label: E
options.text: Only gas bubbles forming below the surface

questions.explanation: Evaporation is escape from the surface. Gas bubbles throughout a liquid are a sign of boiling.

questions.stem: Two identical charges of reactants each theoretically give 80 g product. The first batch yields 75%; combining both batches gives an 80% yield overall. What did the second batch produce?
questions.explanation: The combined actual mass is 0.80 × 160 = 128 g. Subtract the first batch’s 60 g, leaving 68 g.

questions.stem: An insulated cup contains water at 20 °C. After a solid dissolves, the solution stabilises at 16 °C. A separate thermometer confirms that the room stayed at 20 °C. Which statement describes the dissolving process?

options.label: A
options.text: It is exothermic: energy is transferred from the dissolving process to the solution’s thermal store.

options.label: B
options.text: It is endothermic: energy is transferred from the dissolving process to the solution’s thermal store.

options.label: C
options.text: It is endothermic: energy is transferred from the solution’s thermal store to the dissolving process.

options.label: D
options.text: It is exothermic because the room is warmer than the final solution.

options.label: E
options.text: The constant room temperature means the dissolving has no energy change.

questions.explanation: The temperature of the solution falls in the insulated cup, so its thermal store decreases. The dissolving takes in energy and is endothermic.

questions.stem: A student says a reaction goes faster at higher temperature only because particles collide more often. Which observation best shows why that explanation is incomplete?

options.label: A
options.text: The concentration of the reactants is unchanged when heated.

options.label: B
options.text: The fraction of collisions with energy at least equal to the activation energy increases.

options.label: C
options.text: The same products form at both temperatures.

options.label: D
options.text: The particles collide more often at the higher temperature.

options.label: E
options.text: The activation energy is identical at both temperatures.

questions.explanation: More frequent collisions are only part of the explanation. At higher temperature a greater fraction of collisions have enough energy to react, even though the activation energy itself does not change.

questions.stem: The gas reaction X ⇌ 2Y is at equilibrium. Pressure is raised by reducing volume at fixed temperature. Which direction is favoured?

options.label: B
options.text: Neither because the atoms are unchanged

options.label: D
options.text: It cannot reach a new equilibrium

questions.explanation: The equilibrium shifts towards fewer gas particles, the X side. Both directions still occur in the new equilibrium.

questions.stem: A reaction makes 18 cm³ gas in its first 6 s and 12 cm³ more in the next 12 s. Which row gives initial interval rate; mean rate for the full 18 s, in cm³/s?
questions.explanation: The first rate is 18/6. The overall rate uses 30 cm³ and 18 s, not the arithmetic mean of the two rates.

questions.stem: A solution of mass 120 g and specific heat capacity 4 J/(g °C) warms by 5 °C. If this is 80% of the reaction heat, how much heat did the reaction release?
questions.explanation: The solution absorbs 2400 J. This is four fifths of the total, so divide by 0.8.

questions.stem: Each trial puts the same volume of excess acid in a gas syringe setup. Trial A uses 2 g of powdered chalk; B uses a 1 g chalk chip. Trial B reacts more slowly at first and gives 24 cm³ of gas at completion. Which row gives the likely reason for B’s slower start; A’s final gas volume?
questions.explanation: The chip exposes less surface than the larger mass of powder. Acid is in excess, so doubling the chalk doubles final gas volume rather than halving it.

questions.stem: Breaking bonds requires 540 kJ/mol and making bonds returns 610 kJ/mol. Which row gives the forward; reverse enthalpy changes in kJ/mol?
questions.explanation: Forward change is 540 − 610. Reversing the reaction reverses the sign of the enthalpy change.

questions.stem: Two gas samples at the same temperature and pressure have volumes 12 and 36 dm³. What is the ratio of their amounts in moles, smaller to larger?
questions.explanation: Equal gas volumes contain equal amounts at the same conditions. The mole ratio matches the volume ratio.

questions.stem: For X(g) + Y(g) ⇌ 2Z(g), the forward reaction is exothermic. Separately test three changes: 1. compress at fixed temperature; 2. cool at fixed volume; 3. remove X at fixed temperature and volume. Which changes favour Z?
questions.explanation: Compression does not favour either side because both have two gas particles per event. Cooling favours the exothermic forward direction, while removing X favours the reverse direction.

questions.stem: In X₂ + 3Y₂ → 2XY₃, each XY₃ molecule has three X–Y bonds. The reaction absorbs 30 kJ/mol. X–X is 180 kJ/mol and Y–Y is 110 kJ/mol. Find X–Y.
questions.explanation: Breaking bonds costs 510 kJ. Forming six bonds must release 480 kJ for a net input of 30 kJ, giving 80 per bond.

questions.stem: Which formula belongs to an alkane with five carbon atoms?
questions.explanation: Alkanes have the formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. Five carbons require twelve hydrogens.

questions.stem: Which starting molecule can form an addition polymer using its carbon–carbon double bond?
questions.explanation: Propene contains C=C. Opening this double bond allows the monomers to join in addition polymerisation.

questions.stem: A gas relights a glowing splint. Which gas is indicated?
questions.explanation: A glowing splint relights in oxygen. A lit splint producing a squeaky pop is a different test.

questions.stem: A chromatogram’s solvent front moves 60 mm from the start line. Two spots lie 18 and 45 mm from that line. Which row gives their Rf values, nearer first?
questions.explanation: Each Rf uses the same denominator, the distance moved by the solvent. Divide each spot distance by 60 mm.

questions.stem: An alkane C₁₀H₂₂ cracks to a molecule of butane and a single other molecule that is an alkene. Find the second formula.
questions.explanation: Butane removes C₄H₁₀ from the atom balance. The remaining molecule has six carbons and twelve hydrogens.

questions.stem: Why is carbon monoxide produced more readily in a fuel burner with a restricted oxygen supply?

options.label: A
options.text: Nitrogen reacts completely with the fuel.

options.label: C
options.text: Carbon dioxide becomes the only product.

options.label: D
options.text: Hydrogen is absent from all fuels.

options.label: E
options.text: Water prevents carbon from reacting at any temperature.

questions.explanation: When oxygen is limited, some carbon is only partially oxidised. Complete combustion would give carbon dioxide instead.

questions.stem: A solution gives effervescence with dilute acid, and the gas turns limewater milky. A flame test gives lilac. Which row identifies cation; anion?
questions.explanation: Lilac indicates potassium. Carbon dioxide, identified by limewater, suggests a carbonate reacting with acid.

questions.stem: Which treatment aims to reduce viable microorganisms in drinking water without relying on trapping them on a filter?

options.label: B
options.text: Settling sand out of the water

options.label: C
options.text: Adding sodium chloride at typical taste levels

options.label: E
options.text: Removing dissolved calcium by ion exchange

questions.explanation: Chlorine disinfects water. Fluoride is added for a different purpose and is not a replacement for disinfection.

questions.stem: A mixture contains sand and two miscible liquids of boiling points 65 °C and 85 °C. Both liquids must be collected separately. Which order and first liquid collected are appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Filter, then fractionally distil; the 85 °C liquid

options.label: B
options.text: Filter, then use a separating funnel; the 65 °C liquid

options.label: C
options.text: Filter, then use a separating funnel; the 85 °C liquid

options.label: D
options.text: Evaporate to dryness, then filter; the 65 °C liquid

options.label: E
options.text: Filter, then fractionally distil; the 65 °C liquid

questions.explanation: Filter off the insoluble solid. Fractionation of the miscible liquids collects the more volatile 65 °C component first.

questions.stem: A mixture burns completely and contains only 0.10 mol methane and 0.20 mol ethene. Which row gives moles of O₂ used; moles of H₂O formed?
questions.explanation: Methane takes 2 O₂ and gives 2 H₂O per molecule; ethene takes 3 O₂ and also gives 2 H₂O. Multiply by each mole amount and add.

questions.stem: Which structure in a muscle cell is the main site of aerobic respiration?
questions.explanation: Most aerobic respiration in a muscle cell takes place in mitochondria. Ribosomes make proteins rather than releasing energy by aerobic respiration.

questions.stem: A leaf palisade cell and a root storage cell come from the same plant. Which structure would usually be much more abundant in the palisade cell?
questions.explanation: Palisade cells are adapted to absorb light for photosynthesis, so they contain many chloroplasts. A root cell can still have a cell wall and a permanent vacuole.

questions.stem: The concentration of a dissolved substance is the same on both sides of a membrane it can diffuse through. What happens to its molecules?

options.label: B
options.text: They cross in one direction only.

options.label: C
options.text: They cross only if the cell uses energy.

options.label: D
options.text: They all move to one side over time.

options.label: E
options.text: They move across only when the membrane is removed.

options.label: F
options.text: They cross both ways at equal rates.

questions.explanation: Random motion continues, so molecules cross each way. Equal rates mean no net movement, not an end to movement.

questions.stem: A 6 mm cube of agar is cut into 27 equal cubes. All the faces of the small cubes are exposed to a solution. By what factor has the total surface area available for diffusion increased?
questions.explanation: Each small cube has side 2 mm, giving a combined area of 27 × 6 × 2² = 648 mm². The original area was 216 mm², so it triples; the number of cubes is not the surface-area factor.

questions.stem: A culture starts with six plant cells. Each completes three rounds of mitosis and cell division; in each round every cell present divides once. No cells are lost. How many cells are present at the end?
questions.explanation: Each round doubles the whole population, so there are 6 × 2³ = 48 cells. Multiplying six by three ignores that cells produced in earlier rounds also divide.

questions.stem: Two cells with the same diploid chromosome number divide. Cell X completes mitosis and cell division. Cell Y completes meiosis. How do the products compare?

options.label: A
options.text: Y produces twice as many cells, with half as many chromosomes per cell.

options.label: B
options.text: Y produces twice as many cells, with the same number of chromosomes per cell.

options.label: C
options.text: Y produces twice as many cells, with twice as many chromosomes per cell.

options.label: D
options.text: Y produces the same number of cells, with half as many chromosomes per cell.

options.label: E
options.text: Y produces half as many cells, with the same number of chromosomes per cell.

options.label: F
options.text: Y produces half as many cells, with half as many chromosomes per cell.

questions.explanation: Mitosis produces two diploid cells and meiosis produces four haploid cells. Meiosis doubles the number of products relative to mitosis, but halves the chromosome number within each product.

questions.stem: Enzyme X binds substrate P but not substrate Q. Which explanation best accounts for this difference?

options.label: A
options.text: P replaces the active site of X, whereas Q cannot replace it.

options.label: B
options.text: X changes the concentration of P before binding it.

options.label: C
options.text: Q is excluded because catalysts bind products but never substrates.

options.label: D
options.text: X reacts because all enzymes bind only the larger substrate.

options.label: E
options.text: The active site of X is complementary to P but not to Q.

options.label: F
options.text: X is used up by P before it can recognise Q.

questions.explanation: Enzyme specificity depends on how well the substrate fits the active site. It is not a general rule about substrate size, and the enzyme is not consumed in the reaction.

questions.stem: Equal pieces of plant tissue gain 6% in mass in a 0.30 mol/dm³ sugar solution and lose 4% in a 0.55 mol/dm³ solution. Assume percentage mass change varies linearly between these points. At which concentration would there be no net water movement?
questions.explanation: Zero lies 6/10 of the way from +6% to −4%, so the concentration is 0.30 + (6/10) × 0.25 = 0.45 mol/dm³. The midpoint would only work if the two mass changes had equal magnitudes.

questions.stem: Identical enzyme samples are tested at pH 4, 5, 6 and 7. The times to make the same small amount of product are 20, 12, 16 and 24 seconds, respectively. Which conclusion is supported?

options.label: A
options.text: The highest measured rate is at pH 4, and it is twice the rate at pH 7.

options.label: B
options.text: The highest measured rate is at pH 5, and it is half the rate at pH 7.

options.label: C
options.text: The highest measured rate is at pH 6, and it is twice the rate at pH 7.

options.label: D
options.text: The highest measured rate is at pH 5, and it is twice the rate at pH 7.

options.label: E
options.text: The highest measured rate is at pH 7, because it takes the longest to make the product.

options.label: F
options.text: The rate is the same at every pH, because the same amount of product was made.

questions.explanation: The fixed amount of product is made fastest at pH 5, taking half as long as at pH 7. The rate is therefore twice as high, not half as high; pH 5 is the best of the tested values.

questions.stem: Of 120 cells in a growing root tip sample, 18 are in mitosis. Assume the fraction observed in mitosis estimates the fraction of the cell cycle spent in mitosis. The average cycle lasts 10 hours. What is the estimated time spent in mitosis?
questions.explanation: Mitosis accounts for 18/120 = 15% of the cells. The estimate is 15% of 600 minutes = 90 minutes; 510 minutes estimates time outside mitosis.

questions.stem: In genetics, what is an allele?

options.label: B
options.text: A characteristic that can be observed

options.label: C
options.text: A whole DNA molecule and its associated proteins

options.label: F
options.text: A cell containing half the usual chromosome number

questions.explanation: An allele is one version of a gene. The observable characteristic is the phenotype, not an allele.

questions.stem: Two copies of a gene have the same length, but one base differs at a single position. Which statement follows from this observation?

options.label: A
options.text: The two cells must have different numbers of chromosomes.

options.label: B
options.text: A whole additional base must be present in one copy.

options.label: C
options.text: The two copies must produce different phenotypes.

options.label: D
options.text: A base substitution could account for the difference.

options.label: E
options.text: The gene must be expressed in both cells.

options.label: F
options.text: The equal lengths rule out a mutation.

questions.explanation: Replacing one base with another changes the sequence but not the length. A changed sequence need not lead to a different observed phenotype.

questions.stem: Two genetically distinct pea varieties are each grown under low and high light. Under either light level, variety A grows taller than B. Within each variety, plants grow taller under high light. What best explains the pattern?

options.label: D
options.text: Successful mutations in every plant grown under high light

questions.explanation: The varieties differ even at the same light level, consistent with an inherited effect. Changing the light level shifts growth within each variety, showing that the environment also matters.

questions.stem: A coding sequence is read in triplets starting at base 1. Which bases form triplet 9?
questions.explanation: The first eight triplets occupy bases 1–24, so the ninth occupies 25–27. Base 27 is the end of triplet 9, not its start.

questions.stem: A grower repeatedly breeds only plants producing the largest seeds. The starting population contains several inherited seed-size variants. Which outcome is most likely after many generations?

options.label: A
options.text: All seed-size variants remain equally common because the plants started in one population.

options.label: B
options.text: Each generation is genetically identical to the original plants.

options.label: C
options.text: Small-seed variants become more common because small seeds need fewer resources.

options.label: D
options.text: Large-seed variants become more common and some other variants may be lost.

options.label: E
options.text: All plants instantly acquire the same allele for seed size.

options.label: F
options.text: Variants can only change frequency if the climate changes.

questions.explanation: Breeding from a selected subset makes inherited traits of that subset more common and can reduce genetic variation. It changes the frequencies of variants over generations, not the genes of every individual at once.

questions.stem: In a meadow, grazing animals eat mostly smooth leaves. Rough and smooth leaves are inherited traits in a plant species. Rough-leaved plants leave more offspring under grazing. What would natural selection predict?

options.label: A
options.text: Smooth-leaved plants turn rough during their lives and then pass on that change.

options.label: B
options.text: Animals cause new rough-leaf alleles to appear only in the plants they eat.

options.label: C
options.text: The proportion of rough-leaved plants rises over generations.

options.label: D
options.text: Rough leaves become rarer because surviving longer lowers reproduction.

options.label: E
options.text: The proportions must stay the same because the traits are inherited.

options.label: F
options.text: All plants develop rough leaves in the first generation.

questions.explanation: Plants with an existing inherited advantage contribute more offspring, so the rough-leaf trait spreads. Selection does not require individual smooth-leaved plants to change their inherited trait.

questions.stem: A stem cell from adult bone marrow can generate several kinds of blood cell but cannot normally generate every body cell type. Which term describes this range of potential?
questions.explanation: Multipotent stem cells can give rise to a limited range of cell types. Pluripotent cells have broader potential, so producing several blood cell types alone does not show pluripotency.

questions.stem: A mammal has 20 chromosomes in an ordinary body cell, including two sex chromosomes. One normal X-bearing sperm and one normal Y-bearing sperm fertilise separate eggs. What is formed?

options.label: A
options.text: One XX and one XY zygote, each with 9 autosomes.

options.label: B
options.text: One XX and one XY zygote, each with 20 autosomes.

options.label: C
options.text: Two XX zygotes, each with 18 autosomes.

options.label: D
options.text: Two XY zygotes, each with 18 autosomes.

options.label: E
options.text: One XX and one XY zygote, each with 18 autosomes.

options.label: F
options.text: One XY and one YY zygote, each with 18 autosomes.

questions.explanation: Each egg contributes X, so the two zygotes are XX and XY. Fertilisation restores 20 chromosomes per zygote, of which 18 are autosomes; nine is the autosome count in one gamete.

questions.stem: A double-stranded DNA fragment contains 240 nucleotides in total. Across both strands, the ratio of adenine to guanine is 2 : 3. How many G–C base pairs are in the fragment?
questions.explanation: There are 120 base pairs, each containing either one A or one G. Thus 3/5 of 120, or 72, are G–C pairs; 144 counts both nucleotides in those pairs.

questions.stem: In a plant, P gives purple flowers and is dominant to p. A purple offspring from Pp × Pp is chosen at random and crossed with pp. What is the probability its first offspring has white flowers?
questions.explanation: Among purple offspring of Pp × Pp, two thirds are Pp and one third are PP. Only a Pp parent can produce white offspring with pp, and does so half the time, giving 2/3 × 1/2 = 1/3. The original white plants are excluded from the parent choice.

questions.stem: Which blood component helps form a clot at a cut?
questions.explanation: Platelets help initiate blood clotting at an injury. Red blood cells carry oxygen and do not perform the role asked for here.

questions.stem: How do hormones released by an endocrine gland usually reach a target organ in another part of the body?

options.label: A
options.text: They travel along a neurone as electrical impulses.

options.label: B
options.text: They pass through digestive ducts into the target.

options.label: C
options.text: They diffuse directly through all intervening tissues without using the circulation.

options.label: D
options.text: They are carried by red blood cells bound to haemoglobin.

options.label: E
options.text: They are transported through the airways.

questions.explanation: Endocrine glands release hormones into the bloodstream, which carries them to target organs. Nerve impulses are a different signalling mechanism.

questions.stem: In a model alveolus the carbon dioxide concentration is higher in the passing blood than in the air space. The separating surface is thin and permeable. Which observation is consistent with diffusion?

options.label: A
options.text: The blood gains carbon dioxide as it passes the air space.

options.label: B
options.text: Carbon dioxide moves across in only one direction at the molecular level.

options.label: C
options.text: The blood loses carbon dioxide as it passes the air space.

options.label: D
options.text: Carbon dioxide moves only if the surface uses ATP.

options.label: E
options.text: The two concentrations move further apart because of diffusion.

options.label: F
options.text: There is no net movement because the surface is thin.

questions.explanation: The net movement is from higher to lower concentration. Carbon dioxide therefore leaves the blood and enters the air space.

questions.stem: During a short sprint, a muscle continues to use glucose even when the oxygen supply is insufficient for fully aerobic respiration. What changes in the muscle as a result of anaerobic respiration?

options.label: A
options.text: The muscle releases oxygen from glucose.

options.label: C
options.text: All glucose is converted to carbon dioxide and water.

options.label: D
options.text: The rate of respiration must fall to zero.

options.label: E
options.text: The muscle makes ethanol and no lactic acid.

options.label: F
options.text: Glucose is produced from lactic acid as the only product.

questions.explanation: Human muscle can release energy anaerobically by converting glucose to lactic acid. Carbon dioxide and water are the products of complete aerobic respiration, not of this pathway.

questions.stem: During a period without food, a healthy person's blood glucose begins to fall. Which response helps restore it?

options.label: A
options.text: More insulin is released, and the liver stores more glucose as glycogen.

options.label: B
options.text: More glucagon is released, and the liver stores more glucose as glycogen.

options.label: C
options.text: Less glucagon is released, and the liver releases less glucose.

options.label: D
options.text: More glucagon is released, and the liver releases glucose into the blood.

options.label: E
options.text: More insulin is released, causing the blood glucose concentration to fall further.

options.label: F
options.text: Less glucagon is released, and the liver takes up more glucose.

questions.explanation: Glucagon promotes the release of glucose from liver stores when blood glucose is low. Increased insulin would lower blood glucose, reinforcing rather than correcting the original change.

questions.stem: Food still moves along the oesophagus when a person swallows while lying flat. Which process is mainly responsible?

options.label: A
options.text: Diffusion of food through the oesophageal wall

options.label: B
options.text: Absorption by villi in the oesophagus

options.label: E
options.text: Waves of muscle contraction in the oesophagus

options.label: F
options.text: Movement of pancreatic enzymes towards the mouth

questions.explanation: Peristalsis uses coordinated muscle contractions to push food along the digestive tract. It does not rely on a downward path or on absorption through the wall.

questions.stem: Two people with similar cholesterol levels have different risks of cardiovascular disease because their other risk factors differ. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.label: A
options.text: Cholesterol cannot contribute to cardiovascular disease risk.

options.label: B
options.text: Cardiovascular disease is passed from one person to another.

options.label: C
options.text: Cardiovascular disease risk can be influenced by several interacting factors.

options.label: D
options.text: One measured risk factor is enough to determine a person's outcome.

options.label: E
options.text: Differences in risk must come only from inherited factors.

options.label: F
options.text: Changing lifestyle cannot alter cardiovascular disease risk.

questions.explanation: Cardiovascular disease has multiple contributors, so equal values for one factor do not imply equal overall risk. That does not make the equal factor irrelevant.

questions.stem: The blood supplying a muscle contains 20 cm³ of oxygen per 100 cm³ of blood. Blood leaving it contains 12 cm³ per 100 cm³. At a blood flow of 450 cm³/min, how much oxygen does the muscle remove in two minutes?
questions.explanation: The muscle removes 8 cm³ of oxygen per 100 cm³ of blood. In two minutes 900 cm³ passes through, giving 9 × 8 = 72 cm³; 36 cm³ is the one-minute amount.

questions.stem: A person's body temperature rises during exercise in air cooler than their skin. They lose water by sweating. Which responses help correct the rise in temperature and the drop in body water, respectively?

options.label: A
options.text: More skin blood flow; less water reabsorbed by the kidneys

options.label: B
options.text: Less skin blood flow; more water reabsorbed by the kidneys

options.label: C
options.text: Less skin blood flow; less water reabsorbed by the kidneys

options.label: D
options.text: More skin blood flow; more water reabsorbed by the kidneys

options.label: E
options.text: Increased shivering; more water reabsorbed by the kidneys

options.label: F
options.text: Increased shivering; less water reabsorbed by the kidneys

questions.explanation: Widening skin blood vessels helps transfer heat to the surroundings when the skin is warmer than the air. Increased water reabsorption reduces urinary water loss; shivering would add heat rather than remove it.

questions.stem: Four equally spaced heartbeat peaks on a patient's ECG span 2.4 s, measured from the first peak to the fourth. Later the interval between adjacent peaks is 0.60 s. By how much has the heart rate changed?
questions.explanation: Four peaks enclose three intervals, so the original interval is 2.4/3 = 0.80 s and the rate is 75 beats/min. The later rate is 60/0.60 = 100 beats/min, an increase of 25; dividing the original span by four would wrongly give no change.

questions.stem: Which organism is a primary producer in a pond food web?

options.label: E
options.text: An insect larva feeding on pond animals

questions.explanation: The alga uses light energy to make organic material and is a producer. An organism that eats or decomposes that material does not produce it by photosynthesis.

questions.stem: In photosynthesis, which substance supplies the carbon atoms that become part of glucose?
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide provides the carbon that becomes incorporated into glucose. Light provides energy, not atoms.

questions.stem: What feature strengthens mature xylem vessels in a plant stem?

options.label: B
options.text: Living nuclei in each vessel element

options.label: D
options.text: Paired guard cells around each vessel

options.label: F
options.text: A permanent column of dissolved sugar

questions.explanation: Lignin reinforces the walls of the hollow xylem vessels. Guard cells control stomata; they do not reinforce vessels.

questions.stem: A leafy shoot is moved into more humid air. Light, temperature and air movement are unchanged and the stomata stay equally open. Why does transpiration normally fall?

options.label: A
options.text: Humid air makes water move faster out through the stomata.

options.label: B
options.text: The water-vapour concentration difference between the leaf and air becomes smaller.

options.label: C
options.text: The plant cannot absorb mineral ions in humid air.

options.label: D
options.text: The leaf is now warmer because the light level increased.

options.label: E
options.text: Water switches from travelling in xylem to phloem.

options.label: F
options.text: The stomata must close completely in humid air.

questions.explanation: Humid air contains more water vapour, reducing the diffusion gradient from the moist leaf interior. With stomatal opening fixed, this smaller gradient is enough to explain the fall.

questions.stem: Four randomly positioned 0.25 m² quadrats contain 2, 4, 5 and 5 daisies. What is the estimated mean density of daisies?
questions.explanation: The four quadrats cover 1 m² in total and contain 16 daisies. The mean count of four is per quarter-square-metre quadrat, not per square metre.

questions.stem: A plant's photosynthesis rate is measured at the same temperature in four trials. At low light it is 2 units at both low and high CO₂. At high light it is 5 units at low CO₂ and 8 units at high CO₂. Which inference is supported?

options.label: A
options.text: CO₂ limits the rate at low light but not at high light.

options.label: B
options.text: Increasing light raises the rate only at high CO₂.

options.label: C
options.text: Increasing CO₂ raises the rate by the same amount at both light levels.

options.label: D
options.text: Temperature must be the only factor limiting photosynthesis.

options.label: E
options.text: At high light, increasing CO₂ lowers the rate.

options.label: F
options.text: Increasing CO₂ raises the rate at high light but not at low light in these trials.

questions.explanation: The CO₂ change raises the rate from 5 to 8 under high light, but leaves it at 2 under low light. The results do not show that temperature is the only limit; it was kept constant.

questions.stem: Carbon in a tree enters the atmosphere during a woodland fire. Some of that carbon later becomes part of a new seedling. Which pair of processes can account for these transfers, in order?
questions.explanation: Combustion releases carbon from the wood as carbon dioxide. A seedling takes in carbon dioxide and fixes its carbon by photosynthesis; respiration releases carbon dioxide rather than taking it up.

questions.stem: A 100 m² plot contains 30 m² of shade and 70 m² of sun. Quadrat estimates give 8 plants/m² in shade and 2 plants/m² in sun for one species. What is the estimated total number of those plants?
questions.explanation: Estimate the two areas separately: 30 × 8 = 240 and 70 × 2 = 140, giving 380. Using the simple mean of the two densities would incorrectly weight the areas equally.

questions.stem: A shoot takes up water at 0.08 cm³/min for 20 min in still air and at 0.14 cm³/min for 10 min with a fan. Assuming uptake tracks transpiration, what is the mean transpiration rate across the full 30 min?
questions.explanation: The combined uptake is 20 × 0.08 + 10 × 0.14 = 3.0 cm³. Divide by the total 30 min to get 0.10 cm³/min; the simple mean 0.11 gives equal weight to unequal times.

questions.stem: A plant respires at a constant rate, releasing 2 units of CO₂ per hour. In the light it photosynthesises at a rate that uses 5 units of CO₂ per hour; in darkness it does not photosynthesise. What is the net CO₂ exchange over 8 h of light and 16 h of darkness?
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis uses 5 × 8 = 40 units, while respiration releases 2 × 24 = 48 units. The plant therefore releases a net 8 units; respiration occurs in the light as well as in the dark.

questions.stem: A diagram shows a bacterium with a single main chromosome, a membrane, a cell wall and ribosomes. A student wants to add a nucleus and put the chromosome inside it. Why should the student leave the nucleus out?

options.label: A
options.text: A bacterium’s DNA is all stored inside its ribosomes.

options.label: B
options.text: Only the cell wall contains the bacterium’s DNA.

options.label: C
options.text: The chromosome is part of the cell membrane.

options.label: E
options.text: A bacterium’s main chromosome lies in its cytoplasm without a surrounding nuclear membrane.

questions.explanation: Bacterial cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus. Their main chromosome lies in a region of the cytoplasm.

questions.stem: A plant cell with an intact membrane is placed in dilute solution with higher water potential than the cell sap. What initially happens?

options.label: A
options.text: The cell gains water by osmosis.

options.label: B
options.text: The cell loses water by osmosis.

options.label: C
options.text: Water moves in only by active transport.

options.label: D
options.text: Only sugar moves into the cell.

questions.explanation: Water moves down its water potential gradient through the membrane. This does not require energy from respiration.

questions.stem: Which nutrient is hydrolysed by a protease?
questions.explanation: Proteases break peptide bonds in proteins. Starch is acted on by amylase, not protease.

questions.stem: The image of a cell is 24 mm long, and its actual length is 60 µm. Which row gives the magnification; the new image length (mm) at double magnification?
questions.explanation: Convert 24 mm to 24,000 µm before dividing by 60. Double magnification doubles the image length, not the actual length.

questions.stem: Root cells accumulate an ion to a higher concentration than in surrounding soil water. Which mechanism can move it inward against that concentration gradient?
questions.explanation: Active transport uses energy to move solute against its gradient. Osmosis describes water movement, not uptake of the ion.

questions.stem: The same enzyme is tested at 25 °C, heated to 90 °C, then cooled to 25 °C. Its activity stays near zero after cooling. What best explains this?

options.label: A
options.text: Cooling converted the enzyme into substrate.

options.label: B
options.text: Heating permanently altered the shape of many active sites.

options.label: C
options.text: Heating increased ordinary molecular motion permanently.

options.label: D
options.text: The lower temperature always prevents enzyme action.

options.label: E
options.text: A catalyst was used up by an unrelated reaction.

questions.explanation: High heat can denature the enzyme. Once permanently altered, its active site does not recover simply because the sample cools.

questions.stem: A root-tip sample has 30 cells in mitosis and 170 outside it. Which row gives the percentage in mitosis; expected mitotic cells in a representative sample of 600?
questions.explanation: There are 200 cells in the first sample, so 30/200 = 15%. Apply this proportion to 600, not only to the non-mitotic cells.

questions.stem:
Identical enzyme samples each process 12 units of substrate at pH 5 or pH 7, taking 48 s and 24 s. Which statements are correct?

1. The mean rate at pH 7 is twice the rate at pH 5.

2. These tests establish pH 7 as the global optimum.

3. The mean rate at pH 5 is 0.25 units/s.
questions.explanation: The rates are 12/48 and 12/24. Testing two values cannot rule out a higher rate at some other pH.

questions.stem: A 250× image shows two cell centres 15 mm apart. A second image displays the same separation as 36 mm. Find the second magnification.
questions.explanation: The second image enlarges the same actual distance by 36/15 times as much. The multiplier applies to 250, not to the actual separation.

questions.stem: Pieces of identical tissue have percentage mass changes of +12, +4 and −4 at sugar concentrations 0.1, 0.3 and 0.5 mol/dm³. Assume linearity in this range. Which row gives the zero-change concentration (mol/dm³); expected mass change (%) at 0.2 mol/dm³?
questions.explanation: Zero is halfway between the changes at 0.3 and 0.5 mol/dm³. Likewise 0.2 is halfway between 0.1 and 0.3, so the mass change is halfway from +12% to +4%.

questions.stem: A diagram labels the two copies of a gene at the same locus as A and a. The organism looks identical to one with genotype AA. What can be concluded about the A and a individual at this locus?

options.label: A
options.text: It is homozygous because it looks like the AA individual.

options.label: B
options.text: It has only one copy of the gene.

options.label: C
options.text: It has two copies of allele A.

options.label: D
options.text: It is heterozygous regardless of its appearance.

options.label: E
options.text: It has two different genes at the locus.

options.label: F
options.text: Its genotype cannot be described unless its offspring are examined.

questions.explanation: A and a are different alleles of the same gene. Having one of each is heterozygosity; identical appearance does not imply identical genotype.

questions.stem: Which base pairs with cytosine in double-stranded DNA?
questions.explanation: C pairs with G; A pairs with T. Uracil is associated with RNA rather than standard DNA.

questions.stem: A species has 16 chromosomes in its diploid cells. How many chromosomes are in each normal haploid gamete?
questions.explanation: A haploid gamete has one chromosome set instead of two. It therefore has 16/2 chromosomes.

questions.stem: Tall (T) is dominant to short (t). A Tt plant is crossed with a tt plant. Which row gives the probability of tall offspring; the fraction of tall offspring expected to be heterozygous?
questions.explanation: The offspring are Tt and tt in equal proportions. All tall offspring have the genotype Tt because the second parent can contribute only t.

questions.stem: During protein synthesis, what directly determines the order in which a ribosome adds amino acids?

options.label: A
options.text: The total number of chromosomes in the cell

options.label: B
options.text: The order in which amino acids enter the cell

options.label: C
options.text: The order of codons on the messenger RNA

options.label: E
options.text: The number of ribosomes in the cell

questions.explanation: The ribosome reads successive codons on the messenger RNA. The order in which the raw materials arrive does not specify the protein sequence.

questions.stem: Genetically identical cuttings grown at different temperatures produce different leaf sizes. Which conclusion has direct support?

options.label: A
options.text: Leaf size is entirely determined by inherited alleles.

options.label: B
options.text: All the cuttings must have acquired identical mutations.

options.label: C
options.text: The cuttings must belong to different species.

options.label: D
options.text: Leaf size cannot vary within one genotype.

options.label: E
options.text: Growing conditions can influence leaf size.

questions.explanation: Leaf size differs without an initial genetic difference, consistent with an environmental effect. This does not exclude a genetic contribution in other plants.

questions.stem: A population with inherited dark and light body colours moves to a dark habitat. Birds catch proportionally more light individuals, but neither colour changes during life. Which outcome can follow across generations?

options.label: A
options.text: All light individuals immediately turn dark.

options.label: B
options.text: Birds produce the dark allele in light prey.

options.label: D
options.text: The dark trait becomes more common.

options.label: E
options.text: The proportions cannot change because individuals keep their colour.

questions.explanation: Surviving dark individuals can leave a higher share of offspring. Natural selection changes frequencies across generations, not the trait of an individual during its life.

questions.stem:
One strand of a 100-base-pair DNA fragment has 28 A and 22 T bases. Which statements are correct?

1. Exactly 28 base pairs are A–T.

2. Its complementary strand has 28 T bases.

3. The complete fragment has 50 A bases.
questions.explanation: The complement has 28 T and 22 A, so the fragment has 28 + 22 A bases. A–T pairs count both A and T positions on the first strand, giving 50 rather than 28.

questions.stem: Two Aa parents have three independently formed offspring. Allele A gives the dominant phenotype. What is the probability exactly one offspring shows the recessive phenotype?
questions.explanation: Each offspring has probability 1/4 of aa. There are three positions for the one recessive offspring, giving 3 × (1/4) × (3/4)².

questions.stem: A diploid mammal has 32 chromosomes including two sex chromosomes. Which row gives autosomes in one normal egg; autosomes in the zygote after fertilisation?
questions.explanation: Remove the two sex chromosomes from the diploid count to get 30 autosomes. An egg contributes half that number.

questions.stem: Which vessel carries blood directly from the heart to the lungs?
questions.explanation: The pulmonary artery carries blood away from the right ventricle to the lungs. The pulmonary vein carries blood in the return direction.

questions.stem: Two equal volumes of blood have the same percentage oxygen saturation. Sample X contains half as much haemoglobin as sample Y. Ignore dissolved oxygen. How does the amount of oxygen carried by X compare with Y?

options.label: A
options.text: X carries the same amount of oxygen.

options.label: B
options.text: X carries twice as much oxygen.

options.label: C
options.text: X carries one quarter as much oxygen.

options.label: E
options.text: X carries half as much oxygen.

options.label: F
options.text: X carries more than Y, but less than twice as much.

questions.explanation: Equal percentage saturation means the same fraction of the oxygen-binding sites is occupied. Half as much haemoglobin therefore carries half as much oxygen.

questions.stem: Which adaptation most directly speeds diffusion across an alveolar wall?
questions.explanation: Thin walls shorten the diffusion path. Thicker walls or reduced exchange area would slow diffusion.

questions.stem: A resting heart beats 72 times/min and ejects 75 cm³ per beat. After a change it beats 90 times/min and ejects 80 cm³ per beat. Which row gives the initial; final output (L/min)?
questions.explanation: Multiply rate by volume per beat. Convert each result from cm³ to litres by dividing by 1000.

questions.stem: Which feature of the small intestine increases the area available for absorption?
questions.explanation: Villi project from the lining and increase the contact area. A smooth wall would have less area in the same space.

questions.stem: After a meal raises blood glucose, which hormone normally helps lower it?
questions.explanation: Insulin promotes uptake and storage of glucose. Glucagon generally increases blood glucose rather than lowering it.

questions.stem: After a skin receptor detects a painful stimulus, which type of neurone carries the signal towards the spinal cord?
questions.explanation: A sensory neurone carries impulses from a receptor into the central nervous system. A motor neurone carries the output towards an effector.

questions.stem:
When a healthy person’s core temperature rises, which responses help return it towards normal?

1. Increased sweating.

2. Increased skin blood flow.

3. Increased shivering.
questions.explanation: Evaporating sweat removes heat, and increased skin blood flow promotes heat transfer to cooler surroundings. Shivering generates heat and would oppose cooling.

questions.stem: A spirometer records 0.45 L per breath at 16 breaths/min. Later it records 0.60 L per breath at 20 breaths/min. By how many litres per minute does the total volume breathed increase?
questions.explanation: Multiply breath volume by breathing rate in each period, giving 7.2 and 12 L/min. Subtract the initial volume per minute, not just the change per breath.

questions.stem: A model kidney filters 160 L of water in 24 hours and reabsorbs 158 L. Later, daily filtration stays the same and daily reabsorption rises to 159 L. Which row gives the first day’s urine volume (L); its percentage decrease the next day?
questions.explanation: Urine water is filtered minus reabsorbed: 2 L initially and 1 L later. The 1 L fall is measured relative to 2 L, not 160 L.

questions.stem: A mature leaf makes sugars in daylight. A nearby developing seed accumulates some of those sugars. Which route explains the transfer from the leaf to the seed?

options.label: A
options.text: Transport in the xylem from leaf to seed.

options.label: B
options.text: Diffusion through air from leaf to seed.

options.label: C
options.text: Transport in the phloem from seed to leaf.

options.label: D
options.text: Transport in the phloem from leaf to seed.

options.label: E
options.text: Transport in the xylem from seed to leaf.

options.label: F
options.text: Evaporation of sugars at the leaf and condensation at the seed.

questions.explanation: The mature leaf is a sugar source and the growing seed is a sink. Sugars are translocated from source to sink in the phloem.

questions.stem: In the chain grass → mouse → owl, what is the mouse's trophic role?
questions.explanation: The mouse eats the producer and is therefore the primary consumer. The owl eats that consumer and is one level higher.

questions.stem: What happens to a stoma when its guard cells lose enough water to become flaccid?

options.label: E
options.text: It doubles its rate of water loss.

questions.explanation: Loss of turgor causes closure. Wider opening generally requires the guard cells to become more turgid, not flaccid.

questions.stem: A student takes five equal-area quadrats in each of two habitats. The mean is 6 seedlings per quadrat in habitat A and 2 in habitat B. The quadrat area is 0.5 m²; habitats A and B are 5 m² and 15 m² respectively. Which row gives the estimated numbers of seedlings in A and B?
questions.explanation: The densities are 6 ÷ 0.5 = 12 and 2 ÷ 0.5 = 4 seedlings per m². Multiply by 5 and 15 respectively to estimate 60 seedlings in each habitat.

questions.stem: Which change, other factors fixed, usually lowers transpiration from a leaf with open stomata?

options.label: A
options.text: Increasing air movement in dry air

options.label: D
options.text: Raising leaf temperature slightly in dry air

questions.explanation: More humid air reduces the water-vapour concentration gradient from leaf to air. Faster wind can remove humid air next to the leaf and have the opposite effect.

questions.stem: Why does providing more light eventually stop increasing photosynthesis under fixed experimental conditions?

options.label: D
options.text: Water ceases to be a reactant.

questions.explanation: Once light is no longer limiting, a different factor such as carbon dioxide availability can cap the rate. A plateau does not mean the process stops.

questions.stem: After nutrient-rich runoff enters a pond, algae multiply and later die. Why can dissolved oxygen fall as the dead algae break down?

options.label: A
options.text: Decomposers use oxygen in aerobic respiration.

options.label: B
options.text: Decomposers prevent fish from breathing air.

options.label: D
options.text: Dead algae no longer absorb mineral ions.

options.label: E
options.text: An increase in photosynthesis consumes oxygen.

questions.explanation: Microorganisms decomposing the algae use oxygen for aerobic respiration. This can remove oxygen faster than it is replenished; photosynthesis releases oxygen rather than consuming it overall.

questions.stem:
At the same temperature a plant has measured net CO₂ uptake of 2, 6 and 6 units/min at light levels 1, 2 and 3. Which statements are supported by these data?

1. Upscaling light from 2 to 3 increases net uptake.

2. Net uptake is equal at levels 2 and 3.

3. Upscaling light from 1 to 2 increases net uptake.
questions.explanation: Uptake rises from 2 to 6 and then stays at 6. A higher light level need not increase net uptake across the entire range.

questions.stem: Producers gain 18,000 kJ of chemical energy. Primary consumers gain 15% of that energy, and secondary consumers gain 20% of the primary-consumer gain. What is the secondary-consumer gain in kJ?
questions.explanation: The first transfer supplies 2700 kJ. The second transfers 20% of 2700 kJ, not 20% of producer gain.

questions.stem: Two habitats occupy 30 m² and 90 m². Sampled densities are 12 and 4 plants per m² respectively. Which row gives the estimated combined population; overall density (plants/m²)?
questions.explanation: Each habitat contributes an estimated 360 plants. Divide the combined 720 by 120 m²; the two sample densities cannot be averaged equally.

questions.stem: Two cells are observed after a dissolved dye is added outside them. The dye cannot cross an intact cell surface membrane. Cell X stays clear; cell Y gradually becomes coloured throughout its cytoplasm. Which conclusion is directly supported?

options.label: A
options.text: Cell X has no cell surface membrane.

options.label: B
options.text: Cell Y no longer has an effective membrane barrier to the dye.

options.label: C
options.text: Cell Y must lack a nucleus.

options.label: D
options.text: Both cells have concentrated the dye by osmosis.

options.label: E
options.text: The difference proves that cell X has a cell wall.

questions.explanation: The dye entered Y’s cytoplasm despite normally being unable to cross an intact membrane. This shows that the barrier to the dye is no longer effective in Y.

questions.stem: A membrane is permeable to water but not to dissolved sugar. Side A has the higher water potential. What initially happens?

options.label: A
options.text: Net sugar movement from A to B

options.label: B
options.text: Net water movement from B to A

options.label: C
options.text: Net water movement from A to B

options.label: D
options.text: Net sugar movement from B to A

questions.explanation: Water can cross down its water-potential gradient. Sugar cannot cross this membrane even if its concentration differs.

questions.stem: Two substrates have similar sizes, but only substrate X binds well to an enzyme. Why does size alone not predict the result?

options.label: A
options.text: The enzyme has the same affinity for every molecule of a given size.

options.label: B
options.text: Substrate concentration alone determines which shapes fit.

options.label: C
options.text: Only large molecules can be substrates.

options.label: D
options.text: The active site also needs a complementary shape and interactions.

options.label: E
options.text: Binding depends on whether the enzyme is consumed.

questions.explanation: The active site interacts with a complementary substrate; identical size alone need not give a fit. Enzymes are not used up by binding.

questions.stem: Microscope drawing A shows a 90 µm cell as 27 mm long. The same drawing sheet depicts a second cell 18 mm long at the same magnification. Which row gives magnification; actual length of the second cell (µm)?
questions.explanation: Convert 27 mm to 27000 µm, giving 300×. At the same scale, the second cell is two thirds of 90 µm.

questions.stem: Two sets of equal-sized cells take up an ion. Set A has more ion inside than outside but continues to take it up. Set B stops uptake when inside and outside concentrations match. Which process is specifically evidenced in A?

options.label: C
options.text: Movement of water against a gradient

options.label: E
options.text: Active transport against a concentration gradient

questions.explanation: Continued net ion uptake against its gradient needs active transport. B’s observation on its own could be explained by diffusion reaching equilibrium.

questions.stem: One test at 20 °C uses 10 units of substrate in 40 s, and a test at 30 °C uses 12 units in 24 s. Which row gives the two mean rates in units/s?
questions.explanation: Divide the quantity used by the actual time for each test. Comparing the amounts without adjusting time would not compare rates.

questions.stem: A dividing cell has copied its DNA but has not yet separated the chromosome copies. What is the role of separating the copies before cell division ends?

options.label: A
options.text: To give each daughter cell a complete set of genetic information

options.label: B
options.text: To halve the chromosome set in every daughter cell

options.label: D
options.text: To generate a new allele at every locus

options.label: E
options.text: To remove all DNA from the cytoplasm

questions.explanation: The two copies of each chromosome go to separate daughters during mitosis. The chromosome set does not normally halve in mitosis.

questions.stem: A plant strip starts at 8 g. After soaking it weighs 8.8 g in solution X and a comparable 8 g strip weighs 7.6 g in Y. Which row gives the two percentage changes; the solution with lower water potential?
questions.explanation: The changes relative to 8 g are +0.8 g and −0.4 g. Water enters in X and leaves in Y, so Y has the lower water potential.

questions.stem: At pH 6, enzyme A makes 20 units in 10 s and B makes 12 in 4 s. At pH 7 they make 21 in 7 s and 15 in 10 s. Which enzyme is faster at both pH values?

options.label: D
options.text: Both are equally fast at both pH values

questions.explanation: At pH 6 the rates are 2 and 3 units/s, so B is faster. At pH 7 the rates are 3 and 1.5 units/s, so A is faster.

questions.stem: A root-tip sample contains 48 dividing cells out of 240. The cell cycle lasts 15 h and half of dividing cells are in its first mitotic stage. Assuming proportions estimate time fractions, how many minutes does that stage last?
questions.explanation: The stage occupies half of the 48/240 mitotic fraction, so times are one tenth of the 15-hour cycle. Convert 1.5 h to minutes.

questions.stem: What process produces haploid gametes from diploid precursor cells in animals?
questions.explanation: Meiosis halves the number of chromosome sets. Fertilisation restores the diploid number.

questions.stem: A plant with genotype Aa is crossed with an AA plant. If A is completely dominant, what fraction of the offspring show the dominant trait but carry the recessive allele?
questions.explanation: The AA parent always supplies A, so every offspring shows the dominant trait. Only half get a from the Aa parent.

questions.stem: A DNA fragment has 60 base pairs. Exactly 24 are G–C pairs. Which number gives its total thymine bases across both strands?
questions.explanation: The remaining 36 pairs are A–T, and every such pair contributes one thymine. There are 120 bases in total, but not two thymine per pair.

questions.stem: In a plant, round seeds (R) are completely dominant to wrinkled seeds (r). A round-seeded plant is crossed with a wrinkled-seeded plant. Exactly one of their first two offspring has wrinkled seeds. Assume independent inheritance. What is the round parent’s genotype, and what is the probability that the next two offspring are both round-seeded?
questions.explanation: A wrinkled offspring got an r allele from each parent, so the round parent is Rr. Each offspring independently has probability 1/2 of being round, so the probability that both are round is 1/4.

questions.stem: Clones X and Y are grown under the same two nutrient conditions. Heights are X: 6 then 10 cm; Y: 8 then 8 cm. Assuming all other conditions are controlled, which conclusion is supported?

options.label: B
options.text: Nutrient condition affected X, and the size of the response differed between clones.

options.label: C
options.text: Genotype was the only cause of variation.

options.label: E
options.text: Each clone reached the same height in both conditions.

questions.explanation: Only X changes height across conditions. Equal conditions can still give different clone heights, so the pattern is not explained by environment alone.

questions.stem: A double-stranded DNA sample contains 200 bases; 60 are guanine. Which row gives numbers of cytosine; adenine bases?
questions.explanation: Guanine pairs one-to-one with cytosine. That leaves 80 A or T bases, divided equally between the two types.

questions.stem: In a protein-coding messenger RNA sequence, every complete codon contains three bases. A region has 84 bases and no stop codon in frame. How many amino acids does it specify?
questions.explanation: There are 84/3 codons. The absence of an in-frame stop means each of them specifies one amino acid.

questions.stem: In pea plants, R gives round seeds and is dominant to r. An Rr plant is self-crossed. One round offspring is selected at random and crossed with rr. What is the probability that its next offspring is wrinkled?
questions.explanation: Among the round offspring, two out of three are Rr. An Rr selected parent has a half chance of passing r, so the joint chance is 1/3.

questions.stem: A diploid mammal has 24 chromosomes including two sex chromosomes. Sperm X has 11 autosomes and an X chromosome. Which row gives total chromosomes in a normal egg; sex chromosomes of the resulting zygote?
questions.explanation: The egg has a haploid set of 12 including X. Fusion with an X-bearing sperm produces an XX zygote.

questions.stem: Before a dry season, 40% of 100 plants carry a drought-tolerant trait. Half the tolerant plants and one sixth of the others survive. What proportion of survivors has the trait?
questions.explanation: There are 20 tolerant and 10 other survivors. The relevant denominator is all 30 survivors, not the initial 100 plants.

questions.stem: Which type of blood vessel normally carries blood away from the heart?
questions.explanation: Arteries carry blood away, regardless of the blood’s oxygen content. A pulmonary artery still counts as an artery.

questions.stem: A heart valve fails to close completely. How can this reduce the volume delivered to an artery per beat?

options.label: A
options.text: The valve can create more red blood cells.

options.label: B
options.text: Blood becomes unable to carry oxygen.

options.label: D
options.text: The heart no longer needs to contract.

questions.explanation: Valves normally maintain one-way flow. A leak allows part of a contraction’s output to move backwards instead.

questions.stem: During a water shortage, what change helps conserve body water?

options.label: A
options.text: More water is reabsorbed by the kidneys.

options.label: D
options.text: Less water is reclaimed from filtrate.

questions.explanation: Reabsorbing more water returns it to the body. This tends to produce less, more concentrated urine, not a larger dilute volume.

questions.stem: Rider A breathes 0.60 L per breath at 16 breaths/min. Rider B breathes 0.80 L per breath at 12 breaths/min. Which result follows?

options.label: A
options.text: A moves 0.20 L/min more than B.

options.label: B
options.text: Their total ventilation volumes per minute are equal.

options.label: C
options.text: B moves 0.20 L/min more than A.

questions.explanation: Both products are 9.6 L/min. Oxygen uptake would also require information about gas composition or exchange.

questions.stem: A pulse trace shows 10 complete intervals in 8 seconds at rest and 12 intervals in 8 seconds after exercise. Which row gives resting rate; increase in beats/min?
questions.explanation: Ten intervals in eight seconds is 75/min; twelve in eight is 90/min. Subtract to find the increase.

questions.stem: An intestinal lining with reduced surface area absorbs glucose more slowly. Which mechanism links the two observations?

options.label: A
options.text: Glucose molecules in the food become larger.

options.label: B
options.text: The lining produces extra glucose from oxygen.

options.label: C
options.text: Less surface is available for transport across the lining at once.

options.label: D
options.text: The glucose concentration in food must fall to zero.

options.label: E
options.text: Every active transport mechanism must stop.

questions.explanation: A reduction in area limits the sites at which uptake can take place in parallel. It does not require glucose to change size or concentration.

questions.stem: When core temperature falls below normal, how do responses that raise it illustrate negative feedback?

options.label: A
options.text: They make the original decrease larger.

options.label: B
options.text: They keep the temperature permanently below normal.

options.label: D
options.text: They cause the set point to rise with no limit.

questions.explanation: Negative feedback acts against a deviation. Heat-generating responses such as shivering oppose cooling.

questions.stem: A muscle receives 0.75 L blood per minute for 4 minutes. Incoming blood contains 18 cm³ O₂ per 100 cm³ and outgoing blood contains 10 cm³ per 100 cm³. How much O₂ does it extract?
questions.explanation: Three litres of blood pass through, or thirty lots of 100 cm³. Each loses 8 cm³ of oxygen, so multiply 30 by 8.

questions.stem: A reflex arc uses a sensory and a motor neurone linked in the spinal cord. If the motor neurone cannot transmit, which pair of outcomes is expected?

options.label: A
options.text: Both signal arrival and muscle response are lost.

options.label: B
options.text: The response survives without the inward signal.

options.label: C
options.text: The sensory neurone directly makes the muscle contract.

options.label: D
options.text: The spinal cord can receive the signal; the muscle response is lost.

options.label: E
options.text: The receptor changes into an effector.

questions.explanation: The sensory route carries input to the central nervous system independently of the motor output. The effector needs the motor signal.

questions.stem: A model compares 120 L filtered and 118.5 L reabsorbed in one day with 100 L filtered and 99 L reabsorbed the next. Which row gives the two urine volumes; the percentage decrease in volume?
questions.explanation: Subtract reabsorbed water from each filtered volume. The decrease is 0.5 L relative to the first day’s 1.5 L, giving one third.

questions.stem: A cut leafy stalk is stood in coloured water. Later, the colour appears in narrow tubes in the stalk and in some veins of the leaf. Which tissue has the dye most directly traced?

options.label: A
options.text: Phloem, which carries water and mineral ions up from roots.

options.label: B
options.text: Xylem, which carries water up to leaves.

options.label: C
options.text: Phloem, which carries sugars away from leaves.

options.label: D
options.text: Epidermis, which transports water between organs.

options.label: E
options.text: Guard cells, which transport sugars from roots to leaves.

questions.explanation: The dye travels with the water through the continuous xylem vessels from the cut stalk into the leaf veins.

questions.stem: Why can a covered leaf lose stored carbohydrate even when the plant still gets water?

options.label: A
options.text: Respiration can continue while photosynthesis is limited by light.

options.label: B
options.text: Water supplies all the light needed for photosynthesis.

options.label: C
options.text: Respiration produces starch without consuming substrates.

options.label: E
options.text: Stored carbohydrates only move when light reaches them.

questions.explanation: Covering blocks light and reduces sugar production. Respiration can still use carbohydrate, so stores can decline.

questions.stem: A field is half shaded and half sunny. A class wants to estimate the mean number of daisies per square metre, making sure both parts are represented. It will combine twelve equal-sized quadrats by taking their simple mean. Which sampling plan best meets these requirements?

options.label: A
options.text: Randomly choose eight positions in shade and four in sun.

options.label: B
options.text: Choose six places with visible daisies within each half.

options.label: C
options.text: Choose twelve positions at random within the sunny half.

options.label: D
options.text: Choose six quadrat positions at random within each half.

options.label: E
options.text: Place all twelve quadrats along the shade boundary.

questions.explanation: Splitting the sample equally matches the two equal areas, so neither half receives disproportionate weight in the simple mean. Random selection within each half avoids favouring conspicuous patches.

questions.stem: A plant’s net CO₂ exchange is +5 units/min in light and −2 units/min in darkness, where positive means uptake. Which row gives gross photosynthetic uptake in light; respiration release, assuming constant respiration?
questions.explanation: Darkness stops photosynthesis but not respiration, showing respiration releases 2. In light the gross uptake must offset that release and still leave net uptake 5.

questions.stem: A producer stores 2500 energy units and a consumer stores 200 units obtained from it. Which row gives transfer efficiency; energy not stored in the consumer?
questions.explanation: The consumer stores 200/2500 of the original, or 8%. The remainder is 2300 units, not necessarily all lost in one process.

questions.stem: A shoot loses 3 g of mass in 30 minutes in moving air and 2 g in 40 minutes in still air. All other variables are controlled. By what factor is the mean loss rate higher in moving air?
questions.explanation: The rates are 3/30 and 2/40 g/min. Compare these rates rather than the total mass changes over unequal times.

questions.stem: A carbon atom fixed by a leaf later enters a herbivore and is released in expired carbon dioxide. Which process releases it in the herbivore?
questions.explanation: Organic carbon is oxidised in respiration and released as CO₂. Photosynthesis fixes carbon rather than explaining this release.

questions.stem: Four 0.5 m² quadrats in region A contain 4, 8, 6 and 10 plants. Four in B contain 1, 3, 2 and 2. Region A covers 30 m² and B covers 70 m². Estimate the total number of plants.
questions.explanation: The two sampled areas are 2 m² each. Densities are 14 and 4 per m², so the estimated regional totals are 420 and 280.

questions.stem: Net uptake starts at 2 units per hour, then reaches 8 with more CO₂ at the same light level, but stays 2 in a separate test with more light at the original CO₂ level. Which change is supported as relieving a limiting factor in the original conditions?
questions.explanation: Only changing carbon dioxide raised the observed rate. That does not tell us which factor becomes limiting after carbon dioxide increases.

questions.stem: Producers fix 6000 kJ. Herbivores consume 25% of it and store 20% of what they consume. Carnivores store 10% of the herbivore gain. Which row gives herbivore gain; carnivore gain (kJ)?
questions.explanation: First multiply 6000 by one quarter, then by one fifth to get 300. The carnivore gain is one tenth of that amount.

questions.stem: Which structure houses most of a typical animal cell’s DNA?
questions.explanation: Most genetic material is in chromosomes in the nucleus; mitochondria contain only a small fraction.

questions.stem: What feature directly helps a root hair cell to absorb substances from soil?

options.label: A
options.text: An impermeable coating over the entire surface

options.label: B
options.text: An extension providing a large surface area

options.label: C
options.text: A very small contact area with the soil

options.label: D
options.text: The absence of a cell membrane

options.label: E
options.text: A rigid valve preventing ion exchange

questions.explanation: The projection provides a larger surface in contact with soil water, which helps uptake.

questions.stem: An enzyme exposed to high temperature remains slow after cooling to its initial temperature. Which explanation best fits?

options.label: B
options.text: The solution still has the high temperature.

options.label: C
options.text: The substrate made the enzyme multiply.

options.label: D
options.text: The enzyme initially worked only when frozen.

options.label: E
options.text: Cooling must have raised the original temperature.

questions.explanation: High temperature can alter enzyme shape irreversibly. Simply cooling the sample does not necessarily restore the active site.

questions.stem: An image of a bacterium is 36 mm long at 12000× magnification. A second bacterium is 5 µm long. Which row gives the first real length; the second image length at the same magnification?
questions.explanation: Divide 36000 µm by 12000. For the other image, multiply 5 µm by 12000 and convert back to millimetres.

questions.stem: Three identical bags initially contain solute concentrations 1, 2 and 3 units. They have membranes permeable only to water and are immersed in a large bath of the same solute at concentration 2. Which bag initially loses water?
questions.explanation: Water moves from higher to lower water potential. It leaves the most dilute bag for the more concentrated bath; the 3-unit bag gains water.

questions.stem: Which final small molecules result from complete digestion by proteases and associated enzymes?
questions.explanation: Proteins are hydrolysed into amino acids. Fats and carbohydrates require different enzymes.

questions.stem: For an enzyme assay, 50 initial substrate units fall to 35 in ten seconds and then to 30 in the next ten seconds. Which row gives the first and second mean substrate-use rates (units/s)?
questions.explanation: The decreases are 15 and 5 units. Divide each by its own ten-second interval.

questions.stem: Why does working muscle sometimes produce lactic acid despite the body continuing to breathe?

options.label: A
options.text: Breathing necessarily stops when muscles contract.

options.label: B
options.text: Lactic acid is the main product of fully aerobic respiration.

options.label: C
options.text: Oxygen cannot ever enter muscle cells.

options.label: D
options.text: Oxygen delivery may not meet the muscle’s demand for aerobic respiration.

options.label: E
options.text: Muscles cannot use glucose when active.

questions.explanation: When aerobic supply is insufficient, anaerobic respiration can supplement energy transfer and produce lactic acid.

questions.stem: A tissue culture grows from 600 to 900 cells while total cell mass rises from 12 to 15 mg. Which row gives change in cell count; change in mean cell mass?
questions.explanation: Cell count is multiplied by 3/2, but mass only by 5/4. Mean mass is multiplied by (5/4)/(3/2) = 5/6, even though the culture grows overall.

questions.stem: A cubic cell model is split into eight identical smaller cubes, all separated. What is the ratio of total exposed surface area to the original area, and what happens to total volume?
questions.explanation: Each cube has half the edge length and one quarter of the area. Eight such cubes give double the area while preserving volume.

questions.stem: What term describes two different versions of the same gene?
questions.explanation: Alleles are versions of the same gene. A phenotype is an observable characteristic.

questions.stem: Purple pods (P) are completely dominant to green pods (p). Plant X has purple pods, and a grower crosses it with a green-podded plant. All 12 offspring have purple pods. Which conclusion is justified?

options.label: A
options.text: X must be PP because no green offspring were observed.

options.label: B
options.text: X must be Pp because its partner was pp.

options.label: C
options.text: X must be pp because the partner contributed p.

options.label: D
options.text: The offspring could be PP or pp but cannot be Pp.

options.label: E
options.text: X could be PP or Pp; the result does not rule out Pp.

questions.explanation: With a pp partner, all offspring of PP are purple. If X is Pp, purple occurs with probability 1/2 each time, so 12 purple offspring can still occur by chance.

questions.stem: Genetically identical plants differ in leaf size after being raised under two light levels with all other conditions controlled. What does this directly demonstrate?

options.label: A
options.text: Different alleles are necessary for every difference in phenotype.

options.label: C
options.text: An acquired leaf size is always inherited.

options.label: D
options.text: Light changes every gene in the same way.

questions.explanation: The genotypes match, while their controlled environments differ. This is evidence for an environmental influence on the characteristic.

questions.stem: A trait is recessive and both parents are heterozygous. Which row gives probabilities that one particular child is unaffected; that two independently conceived children are both affected?
questions.explanation: The chance of aa is 1/4 per child. Its complement is 3/4 and the probability of two aa outcomes is (1/4)².

questions.stem: An organism’s gametes contain 7 chromosomes. Its zygote divides twice by mitosis to produce four cells. How many chromosomes are in all four cells combined?
questions.explanation: Fertilisation restores 14 chromosomes. Each mitotic daughter retains 14, giving 56 in four cells.

questions.stem: A breeder selects the tallest plants as parents over several generations. What must be true for this to reliably increase genetically determined height?

options.label: A
options.text: Every difference must be due entirely to watering.

options.label: B
options.text: All plants must initially have the same alleles for height.

options.label: C
options.text: Some variation in height must be inherited.

options.label: D
options.text: The selected plants must never reproduce.

questions.explanation: Selection can transmit heritable differences through offspring. A difference caused entirely by growing conditions need not be passed on.

questions.stem: A double strand contains 80 A–T pairs and 20 G–C pairs. Which row gives the percentage of all bases that are thymine; guanine?
questions.explanation: There are 200 bases in 100 pairs. Every A–T pair contributes one T; every G–C pair contributes one G.

questions.stem: A change in one DNA base can leave the final protein unchanged. Which statement could account for this?

options.label: A
options.text: Every change deletes the whole chromosome.

options.label: B
options.text: DNA directly becomes the protein without translation.

options.label: C
options.text: Changing a base always changes every amino acid.

options.label: D
options.text: Two different codons can specify the same amino acid.

options.label: E
options.text: Proteins are made from DNA bases.

questions.explanation: A codon can change without changing its encoded amino acid. Thus a DNA change does not necessarily alter the protein’s sequence.

questions.stem: A bird population already varies in beak size. After a change in food supply, birds with one beak size leave more offspring. Which process could change the frequency of that size in later generations?

options.label: A
options.text: Natural selection if the size differences are heritable

options.label: B
options.text: The birds choosing their own alleles after birth

options.label: C
options.text: Mitosis halving every adult’s chromosome number

options.label: D
options.text: Random fertilisation necessarily removing the trait

options.label: E
